Cognitive Psychology · Theme 5 · Problem 5: Long Distance Zoom

Mental representation & imagery

Dual code, propositions, the imagery debate, scaling, scanning, rotation and the bizarreness effect: every concept, study and example

Dear Sezen,

Problem 5 asks a deceptively simple question: in what format is knowledge stored in your head? When you picture your kitchen, is there something picture-like in your brain, or only a description that feels like a picture? Parts A–C give you the main theories and the classic experiments (zooming, scanning, rotating mental images). Part D then tests the theory on a real memory phenomenon: are bizarre sentences remembered better because we picture them?

Your readings build on each other: Sternberg (pp. 276–282) introduces imagery, Paivio’s dual-code theory and the propositional alternative; Sternberg (pp. 294–298) gives Kosslyn’s scaling and scanning experiments and representational neglect; Matlin walks through the imagery debate with rotation, distance, shape, interference and ambiguous figures; and Besken & Mulligan (2021) uses selective interference to ask whether the bizarreness effect really depends on images.

This matters beyond the exam: how you picture a situation, a team or a change process shapes what you remember and decide, and the bizarreness result is a reminder that what sticks is often what means something unusual, not what is merely vivid.

How to read this platform. The Lessons panel has three tabs: 📖 Full lectures (27 screens, reading by reading, every concept and study), 🎯 Learning objectives (A–C and D, each answered) and 🧠 In-depth questions (the warm-up mind map, A&B&C 1–8 and D 1–5, each with triage and a hidden model answer). On every screen look at the diagram first, read the bullets, say the hook out loud, then open the chips. Numbers marked illustrative only show a shape; all others come from your readings.

— Your professor

📸 The big picture in one paragraph: Think of three ways to store ‘the cat is under the table’. A photo (imaginal/analog code: it looks like the scene), a sentence (verbal/symbolic code: arbitrary words) or a database entry like UNDER(cat, table) (propositional code: pure meaning, neither picture nor words). Paivio says we keep photos and sentences (dual code). Pylyshyn says it is all database entries, and the ‘photo’ feeling is a by-product. Kosslyn tests this by asking people to zoom, scan and rotate their mental photos: if the time it takes behaves like zooming, scanning and rotating real pictures, the mental image is working like a picture (functional equivalence).

📚 Key Terms: read these first

TermPlain-language definition
Mental representationThe form in which knowledge is held in the mind.
Analog (imaginal) codeRepresentation that resembles what it stands for (like an analog clock).
Symbolic (verbal) codeArbitrary symbols (words, numerals) that do not resemble what they stand for.
PropositionThe abstract meaning underlying a relationship among concepts, e.g. UNDER(cat, table).
Functional equivalenceImagery uses the same representations and processes as perception.
Bizarreness effectBizarre sentences/images are remembered better than common ones.
Mental imageryMental representation of things not currently seen or sensed
Dual-code theoryPaivio: knowledge is stored in an imaginal (analog) AND a verbal (symbolic) code
Symbol / symbolic codeArbitrary sign that doesn’t resemble what it stands for (‘9’, words)
EpiphenomenonA by-product of more basic processes; how propositional theory sees images
Predicate calculusShorthand [relation](subject, object) for a proposition, e.g. Bite(mouse, cat)
Imagery debateAre images stored in an analog code (Kosslyn) or a propositional code (Pylyshyn)?

Image scanningScan time increases linearly with distance on a mental map (Kosslyn et al., 1978)
Mental rotationRT increases linearly with rotation angle (Shepard & Metzler, 1971)
Selective interferenceTwo tasks using the same system interfere (Brooks, 1968; Segal & Fusella, 1970)
Experimenter expectancyResearchers’ expectations shaping results; ruled out for scanning
Representational neglectIgnoring half of an imagined scene
Visuo-spatial sketchpadBaddeley & Hitch’s store for visual and spatial information
Dynamic visual noise / spatial tapping / visual spanDistractor tasks that selectively load visual working memory
Sentence access / noun recallRecall measures: ≥ 1 noun of a sentence recalled / proportion of nouns recalled

🧵 Synthesis

One thread runs through Problem 5: to find out what format a representation has, test whether it behaves like that format. Kosslyn showed that mental images behave like pictures (zooming, scanning and rotating take time in proportion to size, distance and angle), and they compete with perception for the same machinery. Besken and Mulligan used the same logic in reverse: if the bizarreness effect were carried by images, knocking out visual imagery should shrink it. It did not, so this effect is probably carried by meaning (verbal/semantic, propositional-like) processing.

Exam tip: always pair a representational claim with the prediction it makes (analog → time grows with distance; propositional → no distance effect; imagery-based effect → reduced by visuospatial distraction) and the result that tests it.

Readings: Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 276–282; 294–298) · Matlin (pp. 211–220) · Besken & Mulligan (2021), JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

Part A · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 276–282)
Lecture 1 of 27 · objectives A1

🖼️ What is mental imagery?

Definition, senses, uses and limits

❓ This lecture answers: What is mental imagery, what do we use it for, and why can’t the mind simply keep a photo of everything?
↳ How it fits: This sets up the theme: since the brain cannot store an exact copy of every image, we have to ask what format images are really kept in.
  • Mental imagery = the mental representation of things that are not currently seen or sensed (Moulton & Kosslyn, 2009); even things never experienced or that don’t exist.
  • Imagery can be in any modality (sound, smell, taste), but research focuses on visual imagery; diaries show far more visual images (Kosslyn et al., 1990).
  • We use images to solve problems (is a cherry or an apple darker red? how many windows in your home?).
  • Applications: guided imagery for pain and immunity, phobias, design and science; better story memory in Down syndrome; occupational therapy after brain damage.
  • People differ in imagery ability (visible with fMRI); the brain can’t store every image as an exact copy, so the format of images is the big question.
🪝 Memory hook: Imagery = seeing without eyes 👁️‍🗨️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Imagery is useful and varies between people, but it can’t be a stored photo of everything we have seen.
Tap to open ▸
Close your eyes and count the windows in your home. You ‘walk through’ a picture in your head. That picture is mental imagery, and psychologists want to know what it’s made of.
ApplicationExample
Problem solvingwhich is darker red, cherry or apple?
Healthguided imagery for pain, immune response, phobias
MemoryDown syndrome: images + story → better recall
Rehabilitationimagining task steps (washing dishes, taking medication)
Professionsarchitects, engineers, physicists, biochemists
Learningimagery practice improves line-asymmetry sensitivity (Tartaglia et al., 2009)

🧩 Comprehension check

Define mental imagery.

The mental representation of things that are not currently seen or sensed by the sense organs.

Why can’t all images be stored as exact copies?

There would be far too many; brain capacity is inadequate for that.

Part A · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 276–282)
Lecture 2 of 27 · objectives A1 · A2

🕰️ Dual-code theory: analog vs symbolic codes

Paivio’s two ways of storing knowledge

❓ This lecture answers: What does Paivio’s dual-code theory claim, and what is the difference between an analog code and a symbolic code?
↳ How it fits: Here the theme’s question gets its first answer: Paivio says the mind keeps both, picture-like codes that resemble things and word-like codes that only stand for them.
  • Dual-code theory (Paivio, 1969, 1971): we represent information with both pictorial and verbal codes.
  • Analog code: resembles the object it represents, just as clock hands are analogous to time passing; mental images are analog.
  • Symbolic code: chosen arbitrarily to stand for something it doesn’t resemble (a digital clock; the numeral ‘9’; words).
  • Abstract concepts like justice and peace are best represented symbolically; a symbol only has meaning because we use it for a deeper concept.
  • Cat demo: questions about shape and size (tail to nose?) use the image; facts (mammal? likes fish?) use symbolic knowledge.
🪝 Memory hook: Analog = looks like it 🕰️; symbolic = stands for it 🔢.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Dual coding means images and words are two separate codes in the mind.
Tap to open ▸
A map of your street looks like your street: analog. The street’s name doesn’t look like anything: symbolic. Paivio says your mind keeps both kinds.
Analog (imaginal) codeSymbolic (verbal) code
Resemblanceresembles the represented objectarbitrary, no resemblance
Metaphoranalog clock (hands)digital clock (numerals)
Examplesimage of a tree or riverthe word ‘tree’, the numeral 9
Best forspatial and visual propertiesabstract concepts (justice, peace), facts
▶ dual coding theory Paivio▶ analog vs symbolic representation(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What makes a code ‘analog’?

It resembles what it represents, preserving its physical or spatial relations.

Why is the numeral 9 a symbolic code?

Nothing about its shape suggests ‘nineness’: it was arbitrarily chosen.

Part A · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 276–282)
Lecture 3 of 27 · objectives A1 · A2

🧪 Evidence for dual coding: Paivio and Brooks

Recall order, concrete words and selective interference

❓ This lecture answers: What evidence shows that pictures and words are stored in two separate systems in the mind?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L2: recall order, concrete words and Brooks’ ‘same lane’ interference give the dual-code view its first real support.
  • Paivio (1969): pictures were recalled better in any order, but the sequence of words was recalled better than the sequence of pictures → two different systems.
  • Concrete words (book, window, hat: easy to visualise) are recalled better than abstract words (peace, harmony): they get two codes.
  • Logic of interference: if two tasks use the same system, doing both slows you down; if they don’t interfere, they use different systems.
  • Brooks (1968): a visual task was slowed by a visual (pointing) response; a verbal task by a verbal (spoken) response; tapping interfered with neither.
  • Conclusion: two distinct codes, imaginal (analog) and verbal (symbolic).
🪝 Memory hook: Same lane = traffic jam 🚗🚗; different lanes = smooth.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Selective interference shows that visual and verbal information use different systems.
Tap to open ▸
Try picturing a letter F and pointing to its corners on a sheet: the pointing gets in the way. Saying ‘yes, no’ out loud doesn’t. Seeing and pointing share a lane; speaking uses another.
📄 Brooks (1968)
ElementDetail
QuestionDo visual and verbal information use separate systems?
MethodParticipants did a visual task (judgements about a briefly shown picture) or a verbal task (judgements about a sentence) and responded by speaking, pointing or tapping; response time measured interference.
FindingsVisual task slowest with pointing; verbal task slowest with speaking.
ConclusionTwo distinct codes: imaginal (analogical) and verbal (symbolic).
Why it mattersClassic support for dual-code theory and the logic later used by Besken & Mulligan.
▶ Brooks 1968 interference▶ concreteness effect memory(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why did Paivio’s order result suggest two systems?

Pictures were better in free recall, but words were better when order had to be preserved.

What interference pattern did Brooks find?

Visual task + pointing response and verbal task + spoken response produced the slowest responses.

Part A · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 276–282)
Lecture 4 of 27 · objectives A4

🔬 Kosslyn: seeing with the mind’s eye

Imagery uses much of the machinery of perception

❓ This lecture answers: Does imagining something use the same brain machinery as actually seeing it?
↳ How it fits: This adds brain evidence to the picture side: if imagining and seeing share over 90% of their brain areas, images look like a kind of seeing.
  • Visual imagery is used to recall details (Mickey Mouse’s ears) and to reason (packing bags into a car boot).
  • Imagery is ‘a lot like’ perception: when classifying parts of seen vs visualised objects, more than 90% of the same brain areas were active.
  • Early visual cortex is activated when the task needs high-resolution detail, not for purely spatial tasks, and more often with stronger scanners.
  • Transforming images: imagining twisting with your hand activates motor areas; imagining an external force doesn’t.
  • Imagery is not one thing: a collection of distinct abilities.
🪝 Memory hook: Mind’s eye = DVD player 📀; real eye = live camera 📷: same screen.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Imagery and perception share most of their neural machinery.
Tap to open ▸
Imagining your friend’s face switches on almost the same brain areas as actually seeing it. Imagery is like replaying a recording on the screen your eyes normally use.
FindingImplication
>90% of the same areas active for seen and imagined objectsimagery ≈ perception (functional equivalence)
early visual cortex only for high-resolution tasksdepends on task demands
motor areas only when imagining rotating by handhow you transform an image matters
several distinct imagery abilitiesimagery is not a single process
▶ Kosslyn imagery perception brain▶ visual cortex mental imagery(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What percentage of brain areas overlapped between seeing and imagining?

More than 90%.

When is early visual cortex activated during imagery?

When the task requires high-resolution detail (e.g. the shape of an animal’s ears), not for spatial judgements.

Part A · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 276–282)
Lecture 5 of 27 · objectives A1 · A2

🧾 Propositional theory

Knowledge as abstract meaning, not pictures or words

❓ This lecture answers: What is propositional theory, and why does it say we store abstract meaning instead of pictures or words?
↳ How it fits: This is the rival answer to L2: images are only by-products, and what the mind really stores is a description of meaning, like ABOVE(table, cat).
  • Alternative to dual coding: the conceptual-propositional theory (Anderson & Bower, 1973; Pylyshyn, 1973, 1984, 2006).
  • We don’t store images or words; images are epiphenomena: secondary by-products of more basic processes.
  • Mental representations resemble propositions (‘mentalese’): the meaning underlying a relationship among concepts.
  • ‘The table is above the cat’, ‘The cat is beneath the table’: many wordings, one proposition, written in predicate calculus: ABOVE(table, cat).
  • Pictures and sentences are both stored as propositions; at retrieval the mind re-creates the image or the words (Clark & Chase, 1972). Anderson & Bower later moved to multiple forms; Pylyshyn still holds the view.
🪝 Memory hook: Proposition = the meaning without the wrapping 🎁.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Propositional theory says one abstract meaning code underlies both images and words.
Tap to open ▸
Whether you see a drawing of a cat under a table or read ‘the cat is under the table’, what you keep is the idea UNDER(cat, table). The picture or the words are rebuilt from that idea when you need them.
Dual-code theoryPropositional theory
Number of codestwo: imaginal + verbalone: abstract propositions
Status of imagesa real code (analog)epiphenomena (by-products)
Key namesPaivioAnderson & Bower; Pylyshyn; Clark & Chase
Retrievalfrom the matching codeimage or words re-created from propositions
▶ propositional theory Pylyshyn▶ imagery debate Kosslyn Pylyshyn(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What is an epiphenomenon?

A secondary, derivative phenomenon produced by more basic processes; here, the experience of an image.

Write ‘A cat is under the table’ in predicate calculus.

For example ABOVE(table, cat) or UNDER(cat, table): [relation](subject, object).

Part A · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 276–282)
Lecture 6 of 27 · objectives A2

📋 Using propositions: Table 7.1

Actions, attributes, positions and categories

❓ This lecture answers: How can one simple format of propositions describe actions, attributes, positions and categories?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L5: it shows how flexible the meaning code is, since any scene or sentence can be built from the same [relation](who, what) blocks.
  • Propositions can describe any relationship: actions, attributes, spatial positions, class membership…
  • Table 7.1 shows each relationship three ways: in words (verbal), as a proposition and as an image.
  • General shorthand: [relationship] (subject element, object element), e.g. Bite (mouse, cat).
  • Propositions combine into complex representations (‘the furry mouse bit the cat, which is hiding under the table’).
  • Predicate calculus is only shorthand, not the literal mental format; and people may use both types (Talasli, 1990).
🪝 Memory hook: [relation](who, what): the grammar of meaning.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Propositions are flexible because any relationship can be expressed and combined in the same format.
Tap to open ▸
Think of propositions as Lego blocks of meaning: BITE(mouse, cat) + FURRY(mouse) + UNDER(cat, table) snap together to build any scene or sentence.
RelationshipIn wordsProposition
ActionA mouse bit a cat.Bite [action] (mouse [agent], cat [object])
AttributeMice are furry.[surface characteristic] (furry, mouse)
Spatial positionA cat is under the table.[vertically higher position] (table, cat)
Class membershipA cat is an animal.[categorical membership] (animal, cat)
▶ propositional representation examples▶ predicate calculus psychology(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

How does Table 7.1 illustrate dual-code vs propositional theory?

The words and image columns are the two codes of dual-code theory; the proposition column is the single abstract code of propositional theory.

Is predicate calculus the literal form of mental representation?

No: it is shorthand to show the underlying meaning.

Part B · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 294–298)
Lecture 7 of 27 · objectives A3 · A4

🔍 Image scaling

Small mental images hide their details

❓ This lecture answers: Does the size of a mental image change how quickly we can spot its details?
↳ How it fits: Here the picture view gets its first test: small images hide their details, just as small objects do in real seeing, which a pure description would not predict.
  • Key idea: we use mental images in ways functionally equivalent to how we use percepts.
  • In perception, details of large objects are easier to see; resolution is limited; zooming in loses the whole.
  • Problem: you can’t control people’s image size directly; Kosslyn (1975) used relative size: imagine a rabbit next to an elephant, a fly, an elephant-sized fly or a fly-sized elephant.
  • Questions about the rabbit were answered more slowly when it was imagined small (next to an elephant or elephant-sized fly).
  • Explanation: a mental screen with limited resolution; walking towards the imagined elephant makes it overflow the screen.
🪝 Memory hook: Small on the mental screen = blurry details 🔍.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Mental images have a size and a resolution, like what we see.
Tap to open ▸
Picture a rabbit next to an elephant: the rabbit is tiny, so you must zoom in to see its whiskers. Next to a fly, the rabbit is big and its whiskers are right there. The extra zooming takes measurable time.
📄 Kosslyn (1975)
ElementDetail
QuestionDoes the size of a mental image affect how quickly we see its details?
MethodParticipants imagined the rabbit with an elephant, a fly, an elephant-sized fly or a fly-sized elephant, then verified features of the rabbit; RT measured.
FindingsSlower for the rabbit beside elephants or elephant-sized flies (rabbit small) than beside flies or fly-sized elephants (rabbit large).
ConclusionImaged size affects access to detail, as in perception.
Why it mattersEvidence for functional equivalence and analog images; answers the fly-sized elephant question.
▶ Kosslyn image scaling rabbit elephant▶ mental imagery zoom experiment(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why use relative size in Kosslyn (1975)?

Because image size can’t be controlled directly; pairing the rabbit with a larger or smaller animal sets its relative size.

What is image ‘overflow’?

Zooming in until the image no longer fits the mental screen, so you must zoom out to see it all.

Part B · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 294–298)
Lecture 8 of 27 · objectives A1 · A3

🐱 Kosslyn (1976): imagery vs propositions across ages

Big parts or distinctive parts?

❓ This lecture answers: When do people answer questions about a cat from an image, and when from stored knowledge?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L7: imagery and knowledge give different answer patterns (big parts versus typical parts), so both codes seem to exist, and children rely on images earlier.
  • First-graders, fourth-graders and adults answered ‘Does a cat have claws / a head?’ with or without imagery instructions.
  • Imagery: everyone was faster for larger attributes (head) than smaller ones (claws).
  • No imagery: fourth-graders and adults were faster for distinctive attributes (claws); size had no effect: propositional/associative knowledge.
  • First-graders were faster for large parts even without instructions: they used imagery spontaneously.
  • Supports functional equivalence and dual coding: imaginal and propositional responses differ, and propositional knowledge develops later.
🪝 Memory hook: Imagery asks ‘how big?’; propositions ask ‘how typical?’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Different codes give different response patterns, and they develop at different rates.
Tap to open ▸
Picture a cat and you find its head faster than its claws: the head is bigger. Answer from knowledge and you find claws faster: claws are what make a cat a cat.
GroupImagery conditionNo-imagery condition
1st gradersfaster for large partsfaster for large parts (spontaneous imagery)
4th gradersfaster for large partsfaster for distinctive parts
Adultsfaster for large partsfaster for distinctive parts; much faster than children
▶ Kosslyn 1976 children imagery▶ propositional knowledge development(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why were first-graders faster for large parts even without imagery instructions?

They spontaneously used imagery, lacking the propositional knowledge.

How do the results support dual-code theory?

Imaginal and propositional responses followed different patterns, and the two abilities developed at different rates.

Part B · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 294–298)
Lecture 9 of 27 · objectives A3 · A4

🏝️ Image scanning

Scanning a mental map takes time in proportion to distance

❓ This lecture answers: Does scanning across a mental map take longer when the two places are farther apart?
↳ How it fits: This strengthens the picture view: scan time grows with distance as on a real map, which a list of facts in the mind could not explain.
  • Key idea: images can be scanned like percepts, with the same strategies and responses.
  • Kosslyn, Ball & Reiser (1978): memorise an island map (hut, tree, lake…), then mentally scan from one named object to another and press a key on arrival.
  • Almost perfectly linear relation: the farther apart the objects, the longer the scan.
  • Replicated with dots and arrows, imagined or seen (Borst & Kosslyn, 2008), and with 3-D arrays of toys (Pinker, 1980).
  • A purely propositional code predicts no distance effect, so the result supports an analog, spatial representation (like Shepard & Metzler’s rotation).
🪝 Memory hook: Longer trip on the mental map = longer travel time 🗺️⏱️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Scan times grow with distance, as they would on a real map.
Tap to open ▸
If your mental map were a list of facts, ‘hut to lake’ would take no longer than ‘hut to tree’. But people take longer for longer distances: they really travel across a picture-like map.
📄 Kosslyn, Ball & Reiser (1978)
ElementDetail
QuestionIs scanning a mental image like scanning a real map?
MethodParticipants memorised a map of an imaginary island, then on hearing an object’s name mentally scanned to it from another object and pressed a key; RT recorded for many pairs.
FindingsAn almost perfectly linear relation between distance and scanning time.
ConclusionThe map was encoded as an image and scanned like a real map.
Why it mattersStrong evidence for analog codes and functional equivalence.

🧪 Demo: scan your mental map

Study the island for 15 s. It then disappears. For each pair, picture the map, ‘travel’ from the first place to the second and click Arrived when you get there.

▶ Kosslyn image scanning island experiment▶ mental scanning distance(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What would propositional theory predict for scan time?

No effect of distance, since propositions don’t preserve metric distances.

Name two replications of the scanning effect.

Borst & Kosslyn (2008) dots-and-arrow task; Pinker (1980) 3-D array of toys.

Part B · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 294–298)
Lecture 10 of 27 · objectives A4

🧭 Representational neglect

When half of an imagined scene disappears

❓ This lecture answers: What happens to imagined scenes in patients who ignore half of the space around them?
↳ How it fits: This adds patient evidence: losing half of an imagined scene suggests images are laid out in space using the same machinery as seeing.
  • Many patients with spatial neglect (ignoring half the visual field) also show representational neglect.
  • Representational neglect: when asked to imagine a scene and describe it, the patient ignores half of the imagined scene.
  • The two often co-occur but can dissociate: a woman without spatial neglect struggled to produce mental images (Peru & Zapparoli, 1999).
  • Described arrays: the left part was not recalled (Logie et al., 2005).
  • Pictures described fully while visible, but the left part was missing when described from memory (Denis et al., 2002).
🪝 Memory hook: Lose half the world 👁️, sometimes also half the imagination 🧠.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Neglect of imagined space shows that imagery uses spatial machinery shared with perception.
Tap to open ▸
Some brain-injured patients describing their town square from memory only mention the buildings on one side, as if the other half of the mental picture has gone.
Spatial neglectRepresentational neglect
What is ignoredhalf of the visual fieldhalf of an imagined scene
Tasklooking at the worldimagining / describing from memory
Relationoften co-occurcan occur independently (Peru & Zapparoli, 1999)
▶ representational neglect Bisiach▶ hemispatial neglect imagery(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Define representational neglect.

Ignoring half of an imagined scene when asked to describe it.

What did Denis et al. (2002) show?

Patients described a whole image while seeing it, but omitted the left part when describing it from memory.

Part C · Matlin (pp. 211–220)
Lecture 11 of 27 · objectives A1

🕰️ A short history of imagery research

From Wundt to behaviourism to cognitive neuroscience

❓ This lecture answers: How did imagery go from a central topic to a banned one and back, and how can researchers study something invisible?
↳ How it fits: This explains the method behind the whole theme: since images cannot be observed, researchers test whether they behave like real objects.
  • Wundt and early psychologists saw imagery as a central topic.
  • Behaviourists (Watson) rejected it as unobservable; Watson argued imagery did not exist. Between 1920 and 1960 North Americans rarely studied it (only 34 articles in the 1950s).
  • Cognitive psychology rediscovered imagery; neuroscience techniques revived it further.
  • Imagery is hard to study (not directly observable, fleeting), so researchers borrowed perception methods: if images resemble objects, judgements about them should resemble judgements about objects.
  • Spatial skills can be trained at any age (Newcombe, 2010), yet are rarely taught in schools.
🪝 Memory hook: Banned by behaviourists 🚫, rescued by cognitivists 🔬.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Researchers study images indirectly: by testing whether they behave like physical objects.
Tap to open ▸
For forty years psychologists weren’t allowed to talk about pictures in the head, because you can’t observe them. Cognitive psychology brought them back by measuring how long it takes to ‘use’ them.
PeriodView of imagery
Wundt (founding years)important topic
Behaviourism 1920–1960unobservable; Watson: does not exist
1950s34 articles on ‘mental imagery’
Cognitive erarediscovered; neuroscience adds tools

🧩 Comprehension check

Why did behaviourists reject imagery research?

Images can’t be connected to observable behaviour.

What general logic do imagery researchers use?

If images resemble physical objects, judgements about images should resemble judgements about real objects.

Part C · Matlin (pp. 211–220)
Lecture 12 of 27 · objectives A1 · A2

⚔️ The imagery debate: analog vs propositional code

Do images resemble perception or language?

❓ This lecture answers: What exactly is the imagery debate, and what does each side claim about how images are stored?
↳ How it fits: This restates the theme’s two answers in Matlin’s words and previews five tests (rotation, distance, shape, interference, ambiguous figures) that the next screens work through.
  • The imagery debate (Kosslyn et al., 2006): do mental images resemble perception (analog code) or language (propositional code)?
  • Analog code (majority view): a representation that closely resembles the object, preserving its physical relations (a triangle’s lines); not literally a picture in the head.
  • Propositional code (Pylyshyn): abstract, language-like, neither visual nor spatial; not English; images can be generated from it.
  • Neuro evidence: primary visual cortex is active in detailed imagery; people with prosopagnosia can neither recognise nor image faces.
  • Matlin: hard to resolve; both are probably partly right, depending on the task. Five lines of evidence follow: rotation, distance, shape, interference, ambiguous figures.
🪝 Memory hook: Analog = sketch ✏️; propositional = description 📝.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The imagery debate asks whether images are picture-like or description-like, and the answer may depend on the task.
Tap to open ▸
Is your memory of a triangle more like a little sketch, or like the note ‘three lines meeting at three corners’? Kosslyn says sketch; Pylyshyn says note.
Analog codePropositional code
Imagery is a close relative ofperceptionlanguage
Formatresembles the object; preserves physical relationsabstract, language-like description
Main proponentsKosslyn; most imagery researchersPylyshyn
Supporting evidencerotation, scanning, scaling, shape, interference, V1 activationReed (1974); ambiguous-figure reversals are hard
▶ imagery debate analog propositional▶ Pylyshyn vs Kosslyn(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Do analog theorists claim there is a picture in the head?

No: the code preserves physical relations, but details never noticed are also missing from the image.

How does prosopagnosia inform the debate?

People who can’t recognise faces also struggle to image faces, suggesting imagery uses perceptual machinery.

Part C · Matlin (pp. 211–220)
Lecture 13 of 27 · objectives A3

🔄 Mental rotation: Shepard & Metzler (1971)

Turning objects in the mind takes time

❓ This lecture answers: Does turning an object in your mind take longer the farther you have to turn it?
↳ How it fits: Test one of the five from L12: rotation time grows steadily with the angle, as with a real object, which supports the picture-like (analog) code.
  • Reasoning: rotating a real object 180° takes longer than 90°; if images work like objects, the same should hold mentally. A ‘daring’ question in the behaviourist climate.
  • 8 participants judged 1,600 pairs of block figures: same (rotated) or different (mirror image)? Dependent variable: reaction time.
  • RT increased linearly with the angle of rotation.
  • 3-D (depth) rotations were as fast as 2-D (picture-plane) rotations: the same straight line.
  • Supports the analog code: a propositional description wouldn’t change with the angle. Replicated many times with letters and other stimuli.
🪝 Memory hook: Twice the turn ↻↻ = twice the time ⏱️⏱️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Mental rotation time grows linearly with angle, as with physical rotation.
Tap to open ▸
To check whether two shapes match, you mentally turn one until it lines up. The more you have to turn it, the longer it takes, exactly as with a real object in your hands.
📄 Shepard & Metzler (1971)
ElementDetail
QuestionDo people rotate mental images like physical objects?
Method8 participants judged 1,600 pairs of 3-D block drawings as same or different (mirror); pairs differed by picture-plane or depth rotations of 0–180°; RT measured.
FindingsRT increased linearly with angle; depth rotations were as fast as picture-plane rotations.
ConclusionImages are rotated through intermediate positions: analog representation.
Why it mattersThe classic and strongest support for analog codes; basis of the web-app experiment (in-depth Q7).

🧪 Demo: mental rotation

Are the two letters the same (just rotated) or mirrored? Answer as fast as you can. 16 trials.

R+R

🧩 Comprehension check

What was the dependent variable?

Reaction time (not accuracy).

Why do linear RTs support the analog view?

A propositional description would take the same time regardless of angle; analog rotation passes through intermediate angles.

Part C · Matlin (pp. 211–220)
Lecture 14 of 27 · objectives A3

🤟 Mental rotation: individual differences and applications

Hands, age, sign language, gender and stroke

❓ This lecture answers: Why are some people faster at mental rotation, and can this skill be trained or used in therapy?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L13: rotation is a real, measurable skill that changes with experience, age and practice, and can even help stroke patients recover movement.
  • Basic rotation findings replicate with letters and other stimuli: smaller rotations are faster.
  • Handedness (Takeda et al., 2010): right-handers recognise right hands faster; left-handers recognise both equally; upright hands faster than upside-down.
  • Older people rotate more slowly; deaf ASL signers are especially good at rotating scenes 180° (they rotate signs constantly).
  • Gender (Sternberg): men mainly right-hemisphere, women both hemispheres plus inferior frontal areas; women’s greater parietal grey matter is linked to more effort; training reduces or removes the difference.
  • Stroke patients watching virtual figures rotate stimulate their motor cortex and regain movement sooner.
🪝 Memory hook: Practice turns the mental wheel faster 🎡.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Mental rotation ability varies with experience and can be trained.
Tap to open ▸
Sign-language users constantly mirror what they see to match their own hands, so they get very good at mental rotation. Practice changes how fast your mind can turn things.

Why are deaf ASL signers good at mental rotation?

They constantly rotate signs by 180° to match the signer’s perspective to their own.

What happens to gender differences with training?

They decrease or even disappear.

Part C · Matlin (pp. 211–220)
Lecture 15 of 27 · objectives A3 · A4

🧠 The neuroscience of mental rotation

Motor cortex, instructions and brain activity

❓ This lecture answers: Which brain areas do the work when we rotate something in our mind, and why do instructions matter?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L13 and L14: the brain areas used depend on how the turning is imagined, so imagery is closely tied to perception and movement.
  • Kosslyn, Thompson et al. (2001): one group rotated a figure by hand, another watched a motor rotate it; then both rotated it mentally (PET).
  • Hand group: primary motor cortex active during mental rotation; motor group: no motor activity.
  • Standard ‘rotate the figure’ instructions: right frontal and parietal lobes (Wraga et al., 2005; Zacks et al., 2001).
  • ‘Imagine rotating yourself around the figure’: left temporal lobe and part of the motor cortex.
  • A subtle change in wording produces a dramatically different brain response.
🪝 Memory hook: Hands-on learning → hands-on brain ✋🧠.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Brain areas used in imagery depend on how the transformation is imagined.
Tap to open ▸
If you learned to turn something with your own hands, your brain ‘uses its hands’ when it imagines turning it. Change the instruction and a different brain network does the work.
ConditionBrain activity during mental rotation
Previously rotated the object by handprimary motor cortex active
Previously watched a motor rotate itmotor cortex not active
Instruction: rotate the objectright frontal + parietal
Instruction: rotate yourselfleft temporal + part of motor cortex

🧩 Comprehension check

What did the PET study show about prior hand rotation?

Those who had rotated the figure by hand used primary motor cortex when rotating it mentally.

How did instructions change brain activation?

Rotating the object activated right frontal/parietal areas; imagining self-rotation activated left temporal and motor areas.

Part C · Matlin (pp. 211–220)
Lecture 16 of 27 · objectives A3

📏 Visual imagery and distance

Scanning time and the experimenter-expectancy objection

❓ This lecture answers: Could the mental-scanning distance effect simply come from what the experimenters expected to find?
↳ How it fits: Test two of the five: even when assistants were told to expect the wrong result, scan time still grew with distance, so the picture view survives this objection.
  • Kosslyn et al. (1978): long scans for far-apart points, quick scans for nearby points; later research shows a linear distance–time relation.
  • Objection: experimenter expectancy: researchers know long distances ‘should’ take longer and may transmit this to participants (Intons-Peterson, 1983).
  • Jolicoeur & Kosslyn (1985b): assistants were unaware of the typical result and were given a convincing but wrong explanation predicting a U-shaped curve.
  • They still obtained the standard linear relation.
  • So expectancy can’t explain the scanning effect: support for analog codes.
🪝 Memory hook: Wrong expectations, right result ✅.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The distance effect survives a direct test of experimenter expectancy.
Tap to open ▸
Critics said ‘you got the line because you expected it’. So researchers told new assistants to expect a U-curve. The data still came out as a straight line.
📄 Jolicoeur & Kosslyn (1985b)
ElementDetail
QuestionCan experimenter expectancy explain the mental-scanning distance effect?
MethodThe island-map experiment was repeated by assistants who didn’t know the usual result and were told to expect a U-shaped distance–time function.
FindingsStandard linear relation: longer distances took longer to scan.
ConclusionExpectancy cannot account for the results.
Why it mattersDefends the analog interpretation of scanning.
▶ experimenter expectancy effect▶ mental scanning Kosslyn replication(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What is experimenter expectancy?

Researchers’ biases and expectations influencing the outcome of a study.

How did Jolicoeur & Kosslyn rule it out?

Assistants were led to expect a U-shaped curve but still found the linear relation.

Part C · Matlin (pp. 211–220)
Lecture 17 of 27 · objectives A3 · A4

🕒 Visual imagery and shape

Mental clocks and the shapes of states

❓ This lecture answers: Do we judge the shapes of imagined clocks and states the same way we judge real shapes?
↳ How it fits: Test three of the five: shape judgements follow the same rules for images and real things, adding to the case for picture-like codes.
  • Paivio (1978): compare the angle between clock hands at two imagined times (3:20 vs 7:25).
  • With similar angles decisions were slow; with very different angles (3:20 vs 7:05) fast, as with real angles.
  • High-imagery participants (standardised tests) decided much faster than low-imagery participants.
  • Shepard & Chipman (1970): similarity judgements of US state shapes from mental images matched judgements made from sketches.
  • Matlin’s summary: rotation, distance and shape judgements are made the same way for images and physical stimuli: support for analog codes.
🪝 Memory hook: Close angles are hard to tell apart, in the eye and in the mind 🕒.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Shape judgements about images follow the same rules as for real shapes.
Tap to open ▸
Picture 3:20 and 7:25: the hands make almost the same angle, so you hesitate. Picture 3:20 and 7:05 and you know at once. That hesitation pattern is exactly what happens with real clocks.
StudyTaskResult
Paivio (1978)compare hand angles on imagined clocksslow for similar angles; high-imagery people faster
Shepard & Chipman (1970)similarity of imagined vs sketched state shapesjudgements highly similar

Why does the mental-clock task support the analog code?

Decision time depends on the difference between angles, as with real stimuli.

What did Shepard & Chipman compare?

Shape-similarity judgements based on mental images of states vs based on sketches.

Part C · Matlin (pp. 211–220)
Lecture 18 of 27 · objectives A4

🚦 Visual imagery and interference

Segal & Fusella and Mast et al.

❓ This lecture answers: Does holding a mental image make it harder to see a real object in the same sense?
↳ How it fits: Test four of the five: imagery competes with seeing for the same resources, and this ‘block the image’ logic is reused later by Besken and Mulligan.
  • Many studies show that a mental image interferes with perceiving a physical stimulus (try holding a face in mind while reading).
  • Segal & Fusella (1970): while imagining a tree, people were worse at detecting a faint blue arrow; while imagining an oboe sound, they detected it fine.
  • Interference is modality specific: same sensory mode → interference.
  • Mast et al. (1999): imagined diagonal lines distorted judgements of a real line’s verticality, like real lines do.
  • Imagery competes with perception for the same resources: the logic later used to try to block imagery with visual distractor tasks (Besken & Mulligan).
🪝 Memory hook: Same channel 📺 = static.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Imagery and perception interfere when they share a sensory modality.
Tap to open ▸
Imagining a tree uses your ‘seeing’ channel, so a faint real arrow gets lost in the noise. Imagining music uses a different channel, so the arrow is easy to spot.
📄 Segal & Fusella (1970)
ElementDetail
QuestionDoes a mental image interfere with perceiving a physical stimulus?
MethodParticipants formed a visual image (tree) or an auditory image (oboe) and then had to detect a faint visual or auditory signal (e.g. a small blue arrow).
FindingsDetection was worse when the image and the signal were in the same sensory mode.
ConclusionImagery uses modality-specific perceptual resources.
Why it mattersSupport for functional equivalence of imagery and perception.
▶ Segal Fusella imagery interference▶ Perky effect imagery perception(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

When did imagery interfere with detecting the arrow?

When participants imagined a visual scene (a tree), not a sound (an oboe).

What did Mast et al. (1999) show?

Imagined lines distorted orientation judgements about a real line in the same way real lines do.

Part C · Matlin (pp. 211–220)
Lecture 19 of 27 · objectives A1 · A2

🦆 Imagery and ambiguous figures

When images behave like descriptions

❓ This lecture answers: Can we find hidden shapes or flip ambiguous figures in a mental image the way we can in a real picture?
↳ How it fits: Here the picture story breaks down: people often store a figure as a description, so they cannot reinterpret it, which supports a role for meaning codes.
  • Reed (1974) worried that imagery may have limitations: perhaps we store some visual stimuli as verbal descriptions.
  • Participants saw a figure (Star of David) and later judged whether a pattern (parallelogram) was part of it.
  • Only 14% correct for the star/parallelogram; 55% across all items, hardly better than chance.
  • Reed: such figures were stored as propositional descriptions (‘two triangles, one up, one down’), which contain triangles but no parallelograms.
  • Ambiguous figures (duck/rabbit) are hard to reinterpret from a mental image: people sometimes use analog and sometimes propositional codes.
🪝 Memory hook: If you stored ‘two triangles’, you can’t find the parallelogram 🔺🔻.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Some images are stored as interpreted descriptions, supporting a role for propositional codes.
Tap to open ▸
If you remember the star as ‘two triangles’, you have the description, not the picture, so the hidden parallelogram isn’t in your memory to find.
📄 Reed (1974)
ElementDetail
QuestionAre complex figures stored as images or as descriptions?
MethodParticipants saw a figure, then after a delay judged whether a second pattern was part of it (half the time it was).
FindingsOnly 14% correct for the Star of David/parallelogram; 55% overall, near chance.
ConclusionFigures are sometimes stored as propositional descriptions.
Why it mattersKey evidence for the propositional side of the imagery debate.
▶ Reed 1974 mental imagery parallelogram▶ duck rabbit mental image reversal(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What percentage found the parallelogram in the Star of David?

Only 14%.

Why does this support a propositional code?

A stored description (‘two triangles’) doesn’t contain the parallelogram, whereas a picture would.

Part D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
Lecture 20 of 27 · objectives D1 · D2

🐕 What is the bizarreness effect?

Bizarre sentences are remembered better, but why?

❓ This lecture answers: What is the bizarreness effect, and why is it usually explained by visual imagery?
↳ How it fits: This brings the theme’s question to a memory effect: do weird sentences stick because we picture them, or because of what they mean?
  • Bizarreness effect: unusual, implausible or bizarre sentences (or pictures) are better remembered than plausible, common ones.
  • An old idea: the Ad Herennium (90 BCE) advised ridiculous images; modern memory books and training still do.
  • Classic test (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986): a mixed list of bizarre (‘the dog rode the bicycle’) and common (‘the dog chased the bicycle’) sentences, image each and rate vividness → better free recall for bizarre.
  • Usually attributed to visual imagery (‘bizarre imagery effect’); some argue it only appears with imagery instructions.
  • Two imagery accounts: bizarre images take more effort/elaboration (more transformations), or they are more distinctive.
🪝 Memory hook: Weird sticks 🧲.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Bizarre material is remembered better; the debate is about whether imagery causes it.
Tap to open ▸
You’ll forget ‘the dog chased the bike’ by tomorrow, but ‘the dog rode the bike’ sticks. The question is whether it sticks because you pictured it or because it is odd in meaning.
Imagery accountClaimPrediction under visual distraction
Effort / elaborationbizarre images need more transformations (Marshall et al., 1979; Wollen & Margres, 1987)less clear: imagery reduced for both item types
Distinctivenessbizarre images are more unique at encoding and retrievalbizarreness effect should shrink

🧪 Demo: the bizarreness effect on yourself

8 sentences will appear for 4 s each. Imagine each one. Then type every sentence (or key words) you remember.

Give an example of a bizarre and a common sentence.

‘The dog rode the bicycle down the street’ vs ‘The dog chased the bicycle down the street’.

What are the two imagery explanations of the effect?

Bizarre images require more effort/elaboration, or bizarre images are more distinctive.

Part D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
Lecture 21 of 27 · objectives D2 · D3

🧩 The controversy: imagery or meaning?

Why a new kind of test was needed

❓ This lecture answers: Why couldn’t earlier studies settle whether imagery causes the bizarreness effect, and what better test was proposed?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L20 and the interference logic of L18: blocking the visual sketchpad while people learn gives a direct test of whether imagery is needed.
  • Some find the effect without imagery instructions (Weir & Richman, 1996; Worthen, 1997), but participants may image spontaneously; Worthen’s non-imagery effect was less than half the size.
  • Anderson & Buyer (1994): imagery ability didn’t predict recall or the effect; people rating images as less vivid showed a larger effect.
  • Alternative: the effect is driven by verbal/semantic elaboration (Hirshman et al., 1989; Kroll & Tu, 1988).
  • Sentences permit both imagery and verbal encoding, so instructions and correlations can’t give a causal answer.
  • Better test: selectively disrupt visual imagery at encoding with tasks that load visual working memory (Baddeley & Hitch’s visuo-spatial sketchpad) but not verbal processing.
🪝 Memory hook: Knock out the eyes of the mind 🙈: does the effect survive?
★ KEY INSIGHT · Selective interference gives a causal test of the imagery hypothesis.
Tap to open ▸
If a recipe only works with eggs, removing the eggs ruins it. Besken & Mulligan ‘remove’ visual imagery with distracting visual tasks: if the bizarreness effect survives, imagery wasn’t the key ingredient.
Earlier approachLimitation
Imagery vs non-imagery instructionspeople may still image spontaneously
Imagery-ability correlationsnot causal
Earlier distraction studiesdid not selectively target visual working memory
Present approachvisuo-spatial distraction during encoding (DVN, spatial tapping, visual span)
▶ selective interference visuospatial sketchpad▶ Baddeley working memory model(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why can’t instruction studies settle the question?

Participants might image spontaneously even with non-imagery instructions.

What should happen to the bizarreness effect under visual distraction if imagery causes it?

It should be reduced or eliminated.

Part D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
Lecture 22 of 27 · objectives D4

📺 Experiment 1: dynamic visual noise

DVN did not shrink the effect; it got bigger

❓ This lecture answers: Does watching flickering visual noise, which jams the mind’s eye, make the bizarreness effect smaller?
↳ How it fits: First test of L21’s plan: blocking imagery did not shrink the effect, a first hint that the advantage comes from meaning, not pictures.
  • DVN: flickering black-and-white squares; disrupts visual imagery and VWM (e.g. eliminates the concreteness effect), leaves verbal processing intact, needs no response.
  • 36 students; 2 (bizarre/common) × 3 groups: DVN (sentences heard), auditory control, visual control (sentences read).
  • Image each sentence, rate vividness (1–5); 3 minutes of maths; free recall scored as sentence access and noun recall.
  • Visual control replicated the effect (.54 vs .32). Under DVN the effect was larger than in the auditory control (.59 vs .30 against .45 vs .39).
  • Surprise: the auditory control showed no bizarreness effect, so later experiments used visual presentation.
🪝 Memory hook: Static on the screen 📺, still remembered 🐕🚲.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Visual noise did not reduce the bizarreness effect.
Tap to open ▸
Even while staring at flickering TV static, which should jam the mind’s eye, people remembered the bizarre sentences better than the common ones.

Part D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
Lecture 23 of 27 · objectives D4

👆 Experiment 2: spatial tapping

An active visuospatial task, a bigger sample, the same result

❓ This lecture answers: Does an active spatial task like tapping a hidden pattern reduce the memory advantage for bizarre sentences?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L22: a stronger, active way of blocking imagery, with more participants, still left the effect intact.
  • Changes from Exp 1: sentences presented visually (the auditory control had shown no effect), an active task instead of passive viewing, and a larger sample (60).
  • Spatial tapping: tap four pegs in a diamond, two taps a second to a metronome, board hidden from view; disrupts visuospatial processing and imagery but not verbal processing.
  • Bizarreness effect in both groups: access .43 vs .26 (tapping), .48 vs .32 (control).
  • No interaction (p = .85 for access): the effect was not reduced by tapping.
  • Vividness RTs were slower under tapping (consistent with disrupted imagery), but vividness ratings were not lower.
🪝 Memory hook: Tap-tap-tap 👆, still remembered.
★ KEY INSIGHT · An active visuospatial task also left the bizarreness effect intact.
Tap to open ▸
People drew a diamond with their finger over and over, which keeps the brain’s ‘spatial sketchpad’ busy. Their memory advantage for bizarre sentences was just as big as without tapping.

Give two reasons for switching from DVN to spatial tapping.

Visual presentation of sentences became possible (needed for a robust control effect), and tapping is an active task that may disrupt VWM more.

Did tapping reduce the bizarreness effect?

Part D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
Lecture 24 of 27 · objectives D4

🔲 Experiments 3 and 4: the visual span task

Active maintenance, with and without imagery instructions

❓ This lecture answers: Does holding a visual pattern in mind remove the bizarreness effect, with or without imagery instructions?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L22 and L23: even a demanding visual memory task lowered recall overall but left the bizarre advantage just as large.
  • DVN was passive and tapping could become automatic, so Exp 3 used a task with active maintenance: keep a 5 × 6 checkerboard pattern in mind while encoding the sentence, then judge same/different.
  • Span accuracy .75 (chance .50), equal for bizarre and common trials: participants really did the task.
  • Exp 3: distraction lowered overall recall (access .33/.20 vs .45/.28), but the bizarreness effect was not reduced (no interaction); same when only correct-span trials are counted.
  • Exp 4: plausibility ratings instead of vividness, in case imagery instructions had ‘overpowered’ the distractor.
  • Same pattern: effect on sentence access (.35/.19 vs .45/.35), lower overall recall, no interaction; noun recall effect only a trend (p = .075).
🪝 Memory hook: Memory got worse overall ⬇️, the bizarre advantage didn’t shrink ↔️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Even a demanding visual working-memory task reduced recall proportionally, not the bizarreness effect.
Tap to open ▸
Holding a checkerboard in mind made people remember fewer sentences of both kinds, like a tax on everything. But bizarre sentences kept the same lead over common ones.

Why was the visual span task a stronger test?

It required active maintenance of visual information on every trial and checked performance trial by trial.

Why did Experiment 4 use plausibility ratings?

To remove explicit imagery instructions, in case they let people image despite the distraction.

Part D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
Lecture 25 of 27 · objectives D4

🧮 Combined, meta-analytic and Bayesian analyses

Turning ‘no difference’ into evidence

❓ This lecture answers: How can the authors show that ‘no difference’ is real evidence that imagery does not drive the effect?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L22 to L24: pooling the data and using Bayes factors (a way to weigh evidence for ‘no effect’) turns the null results into support for a meaning account.
  • Except Exp 1, the evidence was null interactions, and null results need careful checking.
  • Pooled ANOVA (power .98/.95 for an interaction half the original size): main effects of bizarreness and distraction; interaction n.s. (access p = .27, nouns p = .13).
  • Single-paper meta-analysis: bizarreness .31 [.21, .42]; distraction .12 [.02, .23]; interaction n.s. (opposite direction).
  • Bayes factors: BF01 = 11.49 (access) and 13.86 (nouns): strong evidence for the null (≥ 3 favours the null).
  • All analyses converge: visuospatial distraction does not reduce the bizarreness effect.
🪝 Memory hook: BF01 > 3: the ‘no effect’ is real evidence ✅.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Bayesian analysis lets the authors claim positive evidence for no imagery contribution.
Tap to open ▸
A normal significance test can only say ‘we didn’t find a difference’. A Bayes factor of 11 says ‘the data are 11 times more likely if there is no difference than if imagery mattered’.
AnalysisBizarrenessDistractionInteraction
Pooled ANOVAsignificantsignificant (lower recall)n.s. (p = .27 / .13)
Meta-analysis (access).31 [.21, .42].12 [.02, .23]n.s.

▶ Bayes factor explained▶ null hypothesis evidence Bayesian(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What does BF01 = 11.49 mean?

The data are about 11 times more likely under the null (no smaller effect under distraction) than under the imagery hypothesis.

Why were extra analyses needed?

Most evidence was a null interaction, which conventional tests can’t interpret as evidence for no effect.

Part D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
Lecture 26 of 27 · objectives D3 · D4

🎨 Vividness: the puzzle in the data

Lower for bizarre, unchanged by distraction

❓ This lecture answers: Why were bizarre images rated less vivid, and what does that tell us about the imagery explanation?
↳ How it fits: This adds a puzzle that points the same way: bizarre sentences give weaker images yet better memory, so vivid pictures are unlikely to be the cause.
  • Vividness was always lower and slower for bizarre than common sentences (replicating McDaniel & Einstein, 1986 and others).
  • Distraction did not lower vividness ratings (spatial tapping group even rated 3.36 / 4.17 vs 2.82 / 4.06), but vividness RTs were slower under distraction.
  • Authors’ defence: the tasks are validated selective disruptors; slower RTs suggest imagery was impaired; with a between-subjects design participants can’t compare with undistracted imagery.
  • Lower vividness for bizarre items argues against the effort/elaboration version of the imagery account: bizarre is the weaker imagery condition.
  • The distinctiveness version isn’t refuted by the ratings, but it predicts a smaller effect under distraction, which was not found.
🪝 Memory hook: Bizarre images are fainter 🌫️, yet better remembered.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Weaker, slower images for bizarre sentences make an imagery-based explanation less likely.
Tap to open ▸
People said their bizarre images were less vivid and took longer to form them. If vivid pictures were the secret, the common sentences should have won.

🧩 Comprehension check

Why do slower vividness RTs under distraction matter?

Vividness RT is taken to reflect ease of imaging, so slower RTs suggest the distractors did impair imagery.

Which version of the imagery account do low vividness ratings undermine?

The effort/elaboration version: bizarre items produced weaker, not stronger, imagery.

Part D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
Lecture 27 of 27 · objectives D2 · D3

💬 General discussion and conclusions

Meaning, not pictures

❓ This lecture answers: What do the four experiments together tell us about why bizarre sentences are remembered better?
↳ How it fits: This closes the theme: for this memory effect the answer leans to meaning rather than pictures, though imagery is not rejected for everything.
  • Across four experiments, visuospatial distraction never reduced the bizarreness effect; the visual-imagery hypothesis gets little support.
  • Results fit verbal or semantic accounts: the selective distractors leave verbal/semantic processing intact.
  • Why imagery instructions can enlarge the effect: different reading goals. To image a bizarre sentence you must analyse all its parts and relations; to rate plausibility you need less analysis.
  • DVN removes the concreteness effect (an imagery effect) but not the bizarreness effect: they have different bases.
  • The authors don’t reject imagery in general: one effect often credited to imagery may have other bases.
🪝 Memory hook: Bizarre sticks because of what it MEANS, not how it LOOKS.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The bizarreness effect is probably driven by meaning (semantic/propositional) processing rather than visual imagery.
Tap to open ▸
Besken & Mulligan’s answer: you remember ‘the banker floated across the puddle on a newspaper’ because your mind works hard to make sense of it, not because you saw a sharper picture.
