🧩 Comprehension check

What do the authors propose instead of imagery?

Greater verbal or semantic processing of bizarre sentences.

How do the concreteness and bizarreness effects differ?

DVN eliminates the concreteness effect (imagery-based) but not the bizarreness effect, so they have different bases.

🧵 Synthesis

One thread runs through Problem 5: to find out what format a representation has, test whether it behaves like that format. Kosslyn showed that mental images behave like pictures (zooming, scanning and rotating take time in proportion to size, distance and angle), and they compete with perception for the same machinery. Besken and Mulligan used the same logic in reverse: if the bizarreness effect were carried by images, knocking out visual imagery should shrink it. It did not, so this effect is probably carried by meaning (verbal/semantic, propositional-like) processing.

Exam tip: always pair a representational claim with the prediction it makes (analog → time grows with distance; propositional → no distance effect; imagery-based effect → reduced by visuospatial distraction) and the result that tests it.

A–C · Mental representation and imagery
🎯 Learning objective · A1
❓ The question this screen answers
A1
What are the main theories on mental representation?

🧭 In plain words: Name and explain the competing theories of how knowledge is stored (dual-code, propositional, analog vs propositional imagery = the imagery debate, functional equivalence), with the key evidence for each.

  • Dual-code: analog + symbolic (Paivio)
  • Propositional: abstract meaning, images = epiphenomena (Pylyshyn)
  • Imagery debate: analog vs propositional code
  • Functional equivalence: imagery ≈ perception
  • Probably both, depending on task (Matlin)
🪝 Memory hook: Analog clock vs digital clock vs the idea of ‘quarter past three’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The debate is not whether we experience images (everyone agrees we do) but whether images are a separate format or a by-product of propositions.
Tap to open ▸

Mental imagery is the mental representation of things that are not currently seen or sensed (Sternberg et al.). The question is in which format such knowledge is stored. Three positions dominate.

1. Dual-code theory (Paivio, 1969, 1971). We use two codes: analog codes (mental images that resemble what they represent, like the hands of an analog clock) and symbolic codes (arbitrary symbols such as words or the numeral ‘9’, like a digital clock). Evidence: pictures were recalled better in free order, but word sequences were recalled better than picture sequences (Paivio, 1969), suggesting two systems; concrete words (easily imaged) are recalled better than abstract words; and Brooks (1968) found selective interference: a visual task was slowed by a visual (pointing) response and a verbal task by a verbal response, but not vice versa.

2. Propositional theory (Anderson & Bower, 1973; Pylyshyn, 1973, 1984, 2006). All knowledge is stored as propositions: abstract, language-like representations of meaning (‘mentalese’), neither images nor words. Images are epiphenomena: we experience them, but they are by-products of more basic processes. Both pictures and sentences are stored as propositions and the image or sentence is re-created at retrieval (Clark & Chase, 1972).

3. The imagery debate: analog vs propositional code (Kosslyn et al., 2006; Matlin). Most researchers (Kosslyn) hold that images are stored in an analog code that preserves physical and spatial relationships (not literally a picture in the head); Pylyshyn holds a propositional code. Support for analog: mental rotation (Shepard & Metzler, 1971), scanning (Kosslyn et al., 1978) and scaling (Kosslyn, 1975), plus neuroimaging (primary visual cortex active in detailed imagery). Support for propositional: Reed (1974; only 14% found the parallelogram in a Star of David) and the difficulty of reinterpreting ambiguous figures in imagery.

4. Functional-equivalence hypothesis (the modern version of dual coding): we use mental images the same way we use percepts (Sternberg et al.). Matlin concludes that both analog and propositional approaches are probably partly correct, depending on the task, and Anderson and Bower moved to a model with multiple representation formats; people can use both kinds of representation to improve performance (Talasli, 1990).

TheoryKey claimKey evidence
Dual-code (Paivio)Analog images + symbolic wordsOrder recall for words vs pictures; Brooks (1968) selective interference; concreteness
Propositional (Pylyshyn; Anderson & Bower)Abstract meaning only; images are epiphenomenaReed (1974); ambiguous figures
Analog imagery (Kosslyn)Images preserve spatial propertiesRotation, scanning, scaling; V1 activation
Functional equivalenceImagery works like perceptionSame time patterns; interference; neuroimaging
  • Listing theories without evidence.
  • Saying analog theorists believe in a literal picture in the head.
  • Forgetting the term epiphenomenon / Pylyshyn.

A–C · Mental representation and imagery
🎯 Learning objective · A2
❓ The question this screen answers
A2
What is the difference between verbal, propositional, and imaginal representations?

🧭 In plain words: Define each format, show how each would represent the same fact, and explain the defining property (resemblance, arbitrariness, abstract meaning).

  • Imaginal = analog, resembles
  • Verbal = symbolic, arbitrary
  • Propositional = abstract meaning, neither
  • Predicate calculus: relation(subject, object)
  • Many sentences/pictures → one proposition
🪝 Memory hook: Photo, caption, and the index card behind them.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Ask: does the representation look like the thing (imaginal), use arbitrary language (verbal), or only capture meaning (propositional)?
Tap to open ▸

Imaginal (analog) representations resemble what they represent: they preserve physical and spatial properties such as size, distance and shape (Paivio). An image of a cat under a table has the cat literally below the table in the representation. Best for concrete objects and spatial questions (‘Is a cat’s tail long enough to reach its nose?’).

Verbal (symbolic) representations use arbitrary symbols chosen to stand for something they do not resemble (Sternberg et al.): the word ‘cat’ or the numeral ‘9’ has nothing cat-like or nine-like about it. They keep the surface form of language (the specific words, their order) and are best for abstract concepts (justice, peace) and categorical facts (‘Are cats mammals?’).

Propositional representations are abstract representations of the meaning underlying a relationship among concepts, neither in words nor in images (Anderson & Bower, 1973; Pylyshyn). ‘The table is above the cat’, ‘The cat is beneath the table’ and a picture of the scene all share one proposition, written in predicate calculus as [Relationship](subject, object), e.g. above(table, cat). A proposition does not retain the acoustic or visual properties of the words, nor the exact perceptual form of a picture (Clark & Chase, 1972). Propositions can express actions [bite(mouse, cat)], attributes, spatial positions and class membership, and can be combined into complex representations (Table 7.1).

The key contrast: imaginal = resembles; verbal = arbitrary but language-specific; propositional = abstract meaning independent of both language and image. In dual-code theory imaginal and verbal codes are two separate systems; in propositional theory both are re-created from underlying propositions.

ImaginalVerbalPropositional
NatureAnalog: resembles objectSymbolic: arbitrary wordsAbstract meaning
ExamplePicture of cat under table‘The cat is under the table’above(table, cat)
KeepsSpatial/perceptual propertiesWords and their orderRelations only
Best forConcrete, spatial questionsAbstract concepts, categoriesAny relation; flexible
  • Treating propositions as sentences in English.
  • No example in predicate form.
  • Missing that one proposition fits many sentences.

A–C · Mental representation and imagery
🎯 Learning objective · A3
❓ The question this screen answers
A3
What do image scaling, image scanning, and mental rotation studies tell us about the way imagery works?

🧭 In plain words: Describe each paradigm, its result, and what it implies: that images preserve spatial/metric properties and are processed like percepts (supporting analog codes / functional equivalence), plus the main criticism (experimenter expectancy).

  • Scaling: small images → slower detail (Kosslyn, 1975)
  • Scanning: time ∝ distance (Kosslyn et al., 1978)
  • Rotation: time ∝ angle (Shepard & Metzler, 1971)
  • Expectancy ruled out (Jolicoeur & Kosslyn, 1985)
  • Images preserve spatial properties → analog
🪝 Memory hook: Zoom, scroll, rotate: your mental image behaves like a photo on your phone.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The signature of an analog image is time that grows with the size of the mental transformation, exactly as with real objects.
Tap to open ▸

Image scaling (zooming). Kosslyn (1975) had people imagine a target animal next to a large or small one (rabbit + elephant, rabbit + fly, rabbit + elephant-sized fly, rabbit + fly-sized elephant). Details of the rabbit were verified more slowly when the rabbit was imagined small (next to an elephant) than large (next to a fly), as if a mental screen has limited resolution and we must zoom in; zooming in too far makes the image ‘overflow’ (Kosslyn, 1983). Kosslyn (1976): with imagery instructions, all ages answered faster about large features (a cat’s head); without imagery, adults and fourth graders answered faster about distinctive features (claws), while first graders used imagery anyway. Different patterns for imaginal vs propositional processing also support dual coding.

Image scanning. Kosslyn, Ball and Reiser (1978) had people memorise a map of an island (hut, tree, lake) and mentally scan between objects: scanning time increased almost perfectly linearly with distance. Replications: Borst and Kosslyn (2008) found the same linear distance effect whether dots were seen or imagined; Pinker (1980) found it in 3-D arrays. A propositional code would predict no effect of distance. Criticism: experimenter expectancy (Intons-Peterson, 1983). Jolicoeur and Kosslyn (1985) had assistants told to expect a U-shaped function run the study: they still found the linear relation, so expectancy cannot explain it.

Mental rotation. Shepard and Metzler (1971): eight participants judged 1,600 pairs of 3-D block figures as same/different. Reaction time increased linearly with the angle of rotation, and rotations in depth were as fast as in the picture plane. A propositional code would predict no effect of angle. Replicated with letters and hands; elderly people are slower; deaf ASL signers are especially good; Kosslyn et al. (2001) found motor cortex activity only in people who had first rotated the object by hand.

Related evidence: Paivio (1978) mental clocks (similar angles took longer to compare, like real angles) and Shepard and Chipman (1970) state shapes (similarity judgments from images matched those from maps).

What it tells us: mental images preserve metric and spatial properties (size, distance, orientation) and are transformed in continuous, analog steps, just like physical objects and percepts. This supports analog coding and functional equivalence. Matlin adds the caution that imagery may also use propositional codes on some tasks (Reed, 1974).

  • Describing studies without saying what they imply.
  • Forgetting the propositional prediction (no time effect).
  • Not mentioning the expectancy criticism and its rebuttal.

A–C · Mental representation and imagery
🎯 Learning objective · A4
❓ The question this screen answers
A4
What does it mean for imagery to be functionally equivalent to perception?

🧭 In plain words: Define functional equivalence, give the converging evidence (behavioural parallels, interference, brain), and add its limits.

  • Same representations/processes as perception
  • Same time patterns (zoom, scan, rotate)
  • Modality-specific interference (Segal & Fusella, 1970)
  • ~90% overlapping brain areas; V1; representational neglect
  • Limits: reinterpretation, imagery not one thing
🪝 Memory hook: Imagery is playing a DVD on the same screen the camera uses (Kosslyn’s metaphor).
★ KEY INSIGHT · Functional equivalence means imagery is perception run from memory instead of from the eyes.
Tap to open ▸

The functional-equivalence hypothesis states that we represent and use mental images in ways that are functionally equivalent to our representations and uses of percepts: imagery is not identical to perception, but it relies on the same representations and processes, so it should show the same patterns (Sternberg et al.; Kosslyn). If perception is slower for small details, longer distances and larger rotations, so should imagery be.

Behavioural parallels: scaling, scanning and rotation (A3); mental clocks (Paivio, 1978) and state shapes (Shepard & Chipman, 1970) give the same judgment patterns for images and real stimuli.

Interference: if imagery and perception share machinery, they should compete. Segal and Fusella (1970): imagining a tree made it harder to detect a faint visual stimulus (a small blue arrow), but imagining the sound of an oboe did not; interference is modality-specific. Mast et al. (1999): imagined and real line gratings distorted orientation judgments in the same way. Brooks (1968) showed the same logic for visual vs verbal tasks.

Brain evidence: in Kosslyn’s work more than 90% of the same brain areas were activated when classifying parts of seen vs visualised objects; primary visual cortex is active during detailed imagery (Ganis et al., 2009); people with prosopagnosia also cannot image faces. Representational neglect: patients with neglect ignore the left half of an imagined scene (Logie et al., 2005; Denis et al., 2002); it can occur without perceptual neglect (Peru & Zapparoli, 1999).

Limits: imagery is ‘not one thing’ but a set of distinct abilities (Kosslyn); spatial imagery does not always activate early visual cortex; and images are harder to reinterpret than percepts (ambiguous figures; Reed, 1974), which suggests images are partly interpreted, propositional representations. So functional equivalence is strong but not complete.

  • Saying imagery and perception are identical.
  • Only behavioural evidence, no interference or brain data.
  • No limitations.

D · The bizarreness effect
🎯 Learning objective · D1
❓ The question this screen answers
D1
What is the bizarreness effect?

🧭 In plain words: Define the effect, give the classic example and conditions under which it appears.

  • Bizarre > common in recall
  • McDaniel & Einstein (1986): ‘dog rode the bicycle’
  • Strongest in mixed lists with imagery ratings
  • Ancient mnemonic advice (Ad Herennium)
  • Measured by sentence access and noun recall
🪝 Memory hook: You’ll forget ‘the banker dropped the newspaper in the puddle’; you won’t forget ‘the banker floated across the puddle on a newspaper’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Same words, different scene: only the implausibility changes, and memory improves.
Tap to open ▸

The bizarreness effect is the finding that bizarre (unusual, implausible, impossible) material is remembered better than common (plausible, everyday) material. In the standard paradigm, McDaniel and Einstein (1986) presented a mixed list of bizarre sentences (‘The dog rode the bicycle down the street’) and common sentences (‘The dog chased the bicycle down the street’), asked participants to form an image and rate its vividness, and found better free recall for the bizarre sentences. It replicates widely (Hirshman et al., 1989; McDaniel et al., 1995; Geraci et al., 2013) and also occurs for bizarre pictures (Gounden & Nicolas, 2012).

The idea is ancient: the Ad Herennium (90 BCE) recommended ridiculous or fantastic images as memory aids, as do modern memory self-help books and memory training.

Conditions: the effect is strongest with mixed lists (bizarre and common items together) and imagery/vividness instructions. In Besken and Mulligan (2021) it was robust with visual presentation (Exp. 1 visual control: sentence access .54 bizarre vs .32 common), but absent with auditory presentation in a small group, and weaker for noun recall with plausibility ratings (Exp. 4).

  • Not mentioning mixed lists.
  • Confusing bizarre with emotional or vivid.
  • No example.

D · The bizarreness effect
🎯 Learning objective · D2
❓ The question this screen answers
D2
What is believed to be the origin of the bizarreness effect?

🧭 In plain words: Lay out the competing explanations: visual-imagery accounts (elaboration/effort and distinctiveness) vs verbal/semantic elaboration, and say where Besken and Mulligan land.

  • Imagery account: effort/transformations (Marshall et al., 1979)
  • Imagery account: distinctiveness (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986)
  • Verbal/semantic elaboration account
  • Effect without imagery instructions; no link with imagery ability
  • Besken & Mulligan: little role for imagery
🪝 Memory hook: You remember the weird sentence because you had to think ‘wait, how?’, not because you drew it in your head.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The name ‘bizarre imagery effect’ assumes the cause; the evidence points more to making sense of the sentence than picturing it.
Tap to open ▸

Visual-imagery hypothesis (hence the label ‘bizarre imagery effect’). Two versions: (a) elaboration/effort: bizarre images need more effort and more visual transformations to create (changing size or function, giving objects human qualities; Marshall et al., 1979; Wollen & Margres, 1987), so they are encoded better; (b) distinctiveness: bizarre images are more distinctive and stand out at retrieval, even with similar elaboration (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986; Black et al., 2012; Campos et al., 2009). Support: some studies find the effect only with imagery instructions, not with semantic instructions (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986; Burns, 1996).

Verbal / semantic elaboration hypothesis. Bizarre sentences receive more verbal or semantic processing as people try to make sense of them (Anderson & Buyer, 1994; Hirshman et al., 1989; Kroll & Tu, 1988; Weir & Richman, 1996; Worthen, 1997). Support: the effect occurs without imagery instructions (Weir & Richman, 1996; Worthen, 1997), and imagery ability does not predict it (Anderson & Buyer, 1994).

Besken and Mulligan (2021) tested the imagery hypothesis directly by disrupting visual imagery during encoding. Because the effect was never reduced, they conclude that visual imagery plays little role, and the results are consistent with greater verbal/semantic processing of bizarre sentences (they did not test this view directly). Their vividness data also argue against the effort version: bizarre sentences were rated less vivid and took longer to image. Only the distinctiveness version is not directly refuted by the ratings, but it predicts an interaction with distraction that never appeared.

  • Only describing the imagery account.
  • Not distinguishing the two imagery versions.
  • Overstating: the study did not directly prove the verbal account.

D · The bizarreness effect
🎯 Learning objective · D3
❓ The question this screen answers
D3
How is the bizarreness effect related to visual imagery?

🧭 In plain words: Explain why the effect has been linked to imagery, then the evidence that weakens the link, including the vividness data.

  • Traditionally called the bizarre imagery effect
  • Appears without imagery instructions
  • Imagery ability doesn’t predict it
  • Bizarre = less vivid, slower to image
  • Distraction doesn’t reduce it (unlike concreteness effect)
🪝 Memory hook: A blurrier picture that’s remembered better: the memory boost can’t be coming from the picture.
★ KEY INSIGHT · People may picture bizarre sentences, but the picture is not what makes them memorable.
Tap to open ▸

Why it has been linked to imagery. The effect is typically produced with instructions to form an image and rate its vividness; it has been called the ‘bizarre imagery effect’; and some studies found it only under imagery instructions (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986; Cornoldi et al., 1988; Burns, 1996). The idea is that bizarre scenes produce more distinctive or more elaborated visual images.

Evidence against a strong link:

  • The effect also appears without imagery instructions (Hirshman et al., 1989; Weir & Richman, 1996; Worthen, 1997), and in Besken and Mulligan’s Experiment 4 with plausibility ratings instead of vividness ratings.
  • Imagery ability does not predict it; people who rated images as less vivid even showed a larger effect (Anderson & Buyer, 1994).
  • Bizarre sentences are rated less vivid (Exp. 1 visual control: 2.99 vs 3.58; Exp. 2 control: 2.82 vs 4.06) and take longer to image (e.g., 839 vs 752 ms). If bizarre items were imaged more strongly, the opposite would be expected.
  • Disrupting visual imagery with dynamic visual noise, spatial tapping or a visual span task never reduced the effect (D4), whereas DVN does eliminate the concreteness effect, which is imagery-based (Parker & Dagnall, 2009).

Conclusion: although people may form images of bizarre sentences, the memory advantage does not depend on visual imagery. The authors stress they are not arguing against imagery representations in general: imagery is a real format, but this particular effect has another basis.

  • Assuming the effect is imagery-based by definition.
  • Ignoring the vividness ratings.
  • Overgeneralising to ‘imagery doesn’t exist’.

D · The bizarreness effect
🎯 Learning objective · D4
❓ The question this screen answers
D4
What is the effect of a visuo-spatial distractor task on the bizarreness effect?

🧭 In plain words: Describe the logic, the three distractor tasks across four experiments, the results and the combined analyses.

  • Prediction: distraction should shrink the effect
  • DVN, spatial tapping, visual span
  • Effect never reduced (Exp. 1: even larger)
  • Visual span lowers overall recall, not the effect
  • Bayes factors ≈ 11–14 for the null
🪝 Memory hook: Turning off the projector didn’t stop the film, so the film wasn’t coming from the projector.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A selective distractor is a knockout test: knock out imagery, and an imagery-based effect should fall. This one didn’t.
Tap to open ▸

Logic. If the bizarreness effect depends on visual imagery, a concurrent task that selectively disrupts visual working memory and imagery during encoding should reduce the effect (a sentence type × group interaction). Design: sentence type (bizarre vs common) within subjects, mixed lists; group (distraction vs control) between subjects; 3-minute maths filler, then free recall scored as sentence access and noun recall.

  • Exp. 1 (n = 36): dynamic visual noise (flickering black-and-white squares; disrupts visual imagery, leaves verbal processing intact). Sentences heard over headphones. The bizarreness effect was larger under DVN (access .59 vs .30) than in the auditory control (.45 vs .39), the opposite of the imagery prediction.
  • Exp. 2 (n = 60): spatial tapping (tapping four pegs in a diamond to a metronome, out of sight). Robust bizarreness effect, no interaction (F = .035, p = .85).
  • Exp. 3 (n = 32): visual span task (hold a 5 × 6 checkerboard pattern in mind while encoding, then judge same/different; 75% correct). It reduced overall recall, but the bizarreness effect was not reduced (no interaction).
  • Exp. 4 (n = 32): visual span task with plausibility ratings instead of imagery instructions. Same result for sentence access; noun recall showed only a non-significant trend for bizarreness.

Combined analyses. Pooled over 160 participants, the critical interaction was non-significant (access F(1,158) = 1.22, p = .27; noun recall p = .13), and any trend went the opposite way (bigger effect under distraction). Bayes factors BF01 = 11.49 and 13.86 gave strong evidence for the null hypothesis, and a single-paper meta-analysis agreed.

Conclusion: visuospatial distraction has no effect on the size of the bizarreness effect, even when it lowers memory overall, indicating little role for visual imagery.

  • Saying distraction reduced the bizarreness effect.
  • Confusing a drop in overall recall with a smaller effect.
  • Not mentioning the Bayesian evidence for the null.

Draw one map that links the theories, the classic experiments and the bizarreness study.

🪝 Memory hook: Theories in the middle ring, experiments on the outside, arrows that say ‘supports’ or ‘contradicts’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A good mind map shows how studies support or contradict each theory, not just a list of terms.
Tap to open ▸

Centre: how is knowledge mentally represented?

Branch 1, theories: dual-code theory (Paivio: analog + symbolic codes), propositional theory (Pylyshyn, Anderson & Bower: abstract propositions; images are epiphenomena), the imagery debate (analog vs propositional code) and functional equivalence (imagery uses the same processes as perception).

Branch 2, evidence for analog/FE: image scaling (Kosslyn, 1975), image scanning (Kosslyn et al., 1978; Jolicoeur & Kosslyn ruled out expectancy), mental rotation (Shepard & Metzler, 1971), shape (Paivio’s clocks; Shepard & Chipman), interference (Brooks, 1968; Segal & Fusella, 1970), neuro (>90% overlap; representational neglect).

Branch 3, evidence for propositional: Reed (1974) 14% parallelograms; ambiguous figures are hard to reverse in imagery.

Branch 4, application: the bizarreness effect (Besken & Mulligan, 2021) tests whether a memory effect is image-based by selectively disrupting the visuo-spatial sketchpad: no reduction → meaning-based (verbal/semantic, propositional-like).

Arrows to label: ‘supports’, ‘contradicts’, ‘tests’, ‘uses the logic of’ (interference → Besken).

  • Listing terms without labelled links.
  • Forgetting to connect Besken to the imagery debate.
  • Putting all studies on the ‘analog’ side (Reed supports propositional).
🧩 Resources A, B & C
🧠 In-depth question · AB1

Point to the Table 7.1 columns that belong to each theory and explain how the theories differ.

❓ Canvas question AB1, word for word
AB1How are the dual code theory and the propositional theory illustrated in Table 7.1? Explain the difference between the dual code theory and the propositional theory.
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘how illustrated in Table 7.1’ + ‘explain the difference’
Diagnosiscompare two theories using a table
Treatmentmap each column onto a theory, then contrast number of codes, nature of images and retrieval
  • Words + image columns = dual code
  • Proposition column = propositional theory
  • Two codes vs one abstract code
  • Images real vs epiphenomena
  • Predicate calculus is shorthand
🪝 Memory hook: Two columns = two codes; one column = one meaning.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Dual coding stores the same fact twice, as a picture and a word; propositional theory stores it once, as meaning.
Tap to open ▸

In Table 7.1 each relationship (action, attribute, spatial position, class membership) is shown three ways: in words, as a proposition and as an imaginal representation.

Dual-code theory (Paivio) is illustrated by the words column (verbal/symbolic code) plus the imaginal column (analog code): two separate codes, each storing the information in its own format.

Propositional theory (Pylyshyn; Anderson & Bower) is illustrated by the middle column: the relationship is stored once as an abstract proposition, e.g. Bite (mouse, cat), written in predicate calculus as [relationship](subject, object). The words and the picture are just two ways of expressing (re-creating) that underlying meaning.

Difference: dual code = two modality-specific codes (images are a real analog code; Paivio’s evidence: recall order, concrete words, Brooks’ selective interference). Propositional = one amodal code of meaning; images are epiphenomena; both pictures and sentences are stored as propositions and re-created at retrieval (Clark & Chase, 1972).

Note that predicate calculus is only shorthand, not the literal form in the mind, and people may use both kinds of representation (Talasli, 1990).

  • Saying propositions are ‘words’ (they are not language-specific).
  • Not linking the theories to specific columns.
  • Forgetting that images are epiphenomena for Pylyshyn.
🧩 Resources A, B & C
🧠 In-depth question · AB2

Sort the seven terms into a tree: what resembles its object, what doesn’t, and examples of each.

❓ Canvas question AB2, word for word
AB2The resources present an abundance of terminology to describe representations. Draw a schematic in which the following terms are organized in a meaningful way: analog, depictive, mental image, proposition, symbol, verbal, word.
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘draw a schematic … organise the terms’
Diagnosisclassification: analog vs symbolic family of codes
Treatmentsplit by resemblance (analog/depictive vs symbolic), then place examples and levels
  • Analog = depictive
  • Mental image = analog example
  • Symbol: arbitrary
  • Verbal → word
  • Proposition: amodal meaning
🪝 Memory hook: Picture = looks like it; word = stands for it; proposition = what it means.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The main dividing line is resemblance: analog/depictive codes resemble their objects; symbols don’t.
Tap to open ▸

Top split: does the representation resemble what it stands for?

  • Analog = depictive (synonyms): resembles the represented object and preserves its physical/spatial relations (analog clock). Its typical example is a mental image.
  • Symbolic (symbol): arbitrary, chosen to stand for something it doesn’t resemble (‘9’, a digital clock).

Within the symbolic branch: the verbal code is language-specific; its units are words. A proposition is also symbolic but amodal: the abstract meaning underlying a relationship, neither a word nor an image (Bite(mouse, cat)); words (and images) can express propositions.

Link to theories: dual-code theory uses the analog branch (mental image) and the verbal branch (word); propositional theory claims everything is ultimately stored as propositions; the imagery debate is ‘analog vs propositional’ for images.

  • Treating ‘proposition’ and ‘word’ as the same.
  • Making ‘analog’ and ‘depictive’ separate branches (they are synonyms).
  • No organising principle.
🧩 Resources A, B & C
🧠 In-depth question · AB3

Use the analog/symbolic distinction to explain what is unusual about words like ‘buzz’.

❓ Canvas question AB3, word for word
AB3Explain why 'onomatopea' are atypical words.
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘why atypical words?’
Diagnosisapply the analog vs symbolic distinction to a special case
Treatmentstate what a typical word is (arbitrary symbol), then show what is different about onomatopoeia
  • Words are normally arbitrary symbols
  • Onomatopoeia resemble their referent
  • Resemblance = analog property
  • Hybrid: verbal + analog
  • Still partly conventional
🪝 Memory hook: ‘Buzz’ buzzes: a word that sounds like its meaning.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Onomatopoeia are words that partly work like analog codes.
Tap to open ▸

Typical words are symbolic codes: a symbol is arbitrarily chosen to stand for something it does not perceptually resemble (Sternberg et al.). Nothing about the sound of ‘dog’ resembles a dog; nothing about ‘9’ suggests nineness.

Onomatopoeia (buzz, cuckoo, splash, meow) are atypical because their form resembles what they represent: the word sounds like the sound it names. That is the defining property of an analog code.

So onomatopoeia are a hybrid: verbal units (words in a language) with an analog element. They blur the clean dual-code split between symbolic words and analog images.

They are still partly conventional (an English dog says ‘woof’, a Dutch dog ‘waf’), so the resemblance is approximate, not a copy.

  • Defining onomatopoeia without linking it to analog vs symbolic.
  • Claiming they are fully analog (they differ between languages).
🧩 Resources A, B & C
🧠 In-depth question · AB4

Explain why a slower response to the non-matching eagle supports a picture-like representation.

❓ Canvas question AB4, word for word
AB4In a study by Zwaan et al. (2002) the sentence “The ranger saw an eagle in the sky.” was presented to participants, followed by one of the pictures below. The participants’ task was to indicate whether the item depicted in the picture was mentioned in the preceding sentence. Participants took longer to respond to the picture on the left than to the picture on the right. Which type of representation does this finding support and why?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘which type of representation does this finding support?’
Diagnosistheory-testing: what each theory predicts for an RT difference
Treatmentstate the prediction of the analog and of the propositional view, then match the result
  • Both pictures = ‘yes’ answers
  • Only the implied SHAPE differs
  • Propositions don’t code shape → no difference
  • Analog simulation → mismatch slows
  • Supports analog / functional equivalence
🪝 Memory hook: The mind pictured a flying eagle, so a sitting eagle looked ‘wrong’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Language comprehension seems to create picture-like simulations that include details never stated.
Tap to open ▸

Both pictures show an eagle, so for the yes/no question (‘was it mentioned?’) the correct answer is ‘yes’ both times. The only difference is the shape: the sentence implies a flying eagle with spread wings; the slower picture (left) showed an eagle with a different shape (wings folded/perched).

Propositional prediction: the sentence is stored as abstract meaning, e.g. SEE(ranger, eagle), LOCATION(eagle, sky). Wing shape is not part of that meaning, so both pictures should be verified equally fast.

Analog/perceptual prediction: readers build a picture-like (analog) simulation of the scene, including the eagle’s implied shape. A picture that mismatches the simulation conflicts with it, so verification is slower.

Result: slower for the mismatching picture → supports an analog (imaginal) representation and functional equivalence (imagery and perception share representations). It fits dual coding too, but is hard to explain with a purely propositional code.

  • Saying it supports propositions because the task is verbal.
  • Not stating what each theory predicts.
  • Forgetting that both pictures require a ‘yes’.
🧩 Resources A, B & C
🧠 In-depth question · AB5

Say which representation works most like data in a computer, and why.

❓ Canvas question AB5, word for word
AB5Which type of representation fits best with the computer metaphor that guided a lot of theorizing about cognitive psychology in the last century?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘which type fits the computer metaphor?’
Diagnosismatch a theory to a metaphor
Treatmentname what computers do (symbol manipulation by rules), then find the representation with those properties
  • Computer = rules over discrete symbols
  • Propositions = abstract symbol structures
  • Predicate calculus ≈ program syntax
  • One format for all data
  • Analog images fit less well
🪝 Memory hook: Computers store BITE(mouse, cat), not pictures of mice.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The propositional code is the mind’s machine code in the computer metaphor.
Tap to open ▸

The 20th-century computer metaphor sees the mind as an information processor that manipulates discrete symbols according to formal rules (cf. Newell & Simon’s simulations).

Propositional representations fit best: abstract, amodal, language-like symbol structures (‘mentalese’) with a clear syntax, [relation](subject, object), exactly like statements in a program. Pylyshyn, the main propositionalist, explicitly argued for this computational view.

One format can store both pictures and sentences (as a computer stores any data as code); images are by-products of computation (epiphenomena).

Analog images, which are rotated and scanned through intermediate states, fit an analog device better than a digital computer; that is partly why the imagery debate was so heated.

  • Answering ‘verbal code’ (words are language-specific; propositions are not).
  • Not explaining what the computer metaphor is.
🧩 Resources A, B & C
🧠 In-depth question · AB6

Explain which animal looks more detailed in your image and why that supports functional equivalence.

❓ Canvas question AB6, word for word
AB6Imagine a fly-sized elephant standing next to a rabbit-sized ant. Which animal does your mind’s eye see in more detail and what does this tell you about the functional equivalence hypothesis?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘which do you see in more detail … what does it tell you about FE?’
Diagnosisimage scaling (Kosslyn, 1975)
Treatmentanswer with image size, cite Kosslyn’s animal pairs, explain what FE predicts
  • Ant: larger in the image
  • Imagined size, not real size, counts
  • Kosslyn (1975) animal pairs
  • FE: images used like percepts
  • Propositions predict no size effect
🪝 Memory hook: Big on the mental screen = sharp; small = blurry.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Detail in an image depends on how big the thing is on the mental screen, exactly as in vision.
Tap to open ▸

You see the ant in more detail: it occupies a larger part of the image than the fly-sized elephant, even though real ants are tiny and real elephants huge.

This mirrors Kosslyn (1975): questions about a rabbit were answered more slowly when it was imagined next to an elephant or elephant-sized fly (small in the image) than next to a fly or a fly-sized elephant (large in the image).

Functional equivalence hypothesis: we use mental images the same way we use percepts. In perception, details of large (near) objects are easier to see; resolution is limited. The same applies to the ‘mental screen’: subjective image size, not knowledge about the object, determines access to detail.

A purely propositional code (‘ANT has antennae’) would make the fact equally accessible regardless of imagined size, so the effect supports analog, perception-like images.

  • Answering ‘the elephant, because elephants are bigger’.
  • Not citing Kosslyn’s study.
  • Not defining functional equivalence.
🧩 Resources A, B & C
🧠 In-depth question · AB7

Compare your own reaction times at 0°, 90° and 180° with the classic linear rotation result.

❓ Canvas question AB7, word for word
AB7Conduct an experiment on mental rotation yourself using this web application (settings: 3 rotation angles; 5 trials/condition). In the experiment, you will see the letter R show up to the left and right of the fixation cross (+) and you must determine as quickly and as accurately as possible whether these two Rs are the same or whether they are mirrored (Z = same, M = mirrored; no practice trials). Inspect the results. Are they in line with the results of earlier mental rotation studies? Why (not)?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘inspect the results … in line with earlier studies? why (not)?’
Diagnosisreplication of Shepard & Metzler (1971)
Treatmentstate the expected pattern (RT ∝ angle), compare your own data, explain deviations with design features
  • Expect RT rising ~linearly with angle
  • Matches Shepard & Metzler → analog
  • Few trials → noisy means
  • No practice, only 3 angles
  • Strategies can bypass rotation
🪝 Memory hook: More turn, more time ↻⏱️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A small, noisy experiment can still show the rotation effect, but design limits explain deviations.
Tap to open ▸

Expected pattern (Shepard & Metzler, 1971; replicated with letters, e.g. Cooper & Shepard): reaction time increases roughly linearly with the angle between the two Rs, so 0° < 90° < 180°; error rates often rise with angle too. Mirror judgements require rotating one R into alignment first.

If your data show this, they are in line with earlier research and support the analog view: you rotate the image through intermediate positions.

Reasons your data might deviate: only 5 trials per condition (one slow trial distorts a mean); no practice (early trials slow, learning effects); only three angles (hard to judge linearity); letters can be solved with feature strategies (‘where is the tail?’) rather than rotation; mixing ‘same’ and ‘mirror’ trials; fatigue, distraction or pressing the wrong key.

Good practice: look at correct ‘same’ trials, use medians, and compare with your group’s pooled data.

  • Only describing your numbers without comparing to theory.
  • Ignoring the tiny number of trials.
  • Forgetting why linear RTs support the analog code.
🧩 Resources A, B & C
🧠 In-depth question · AB8

Decide whether longer travel for ‘80 miles’ shows a picture-like map, given that the maps looked identical.

❓ Canvas question AB8, word for word
AB8In one experiment, participants studied a map that depicted (among other things) a sandy bay and a telephone mast. On the map of half of the participants, the distance between the bay and the mast was indicated as 20 miles. On the map of the other half of the participants, it was indicated as 80 miles. Except for the number that indicated the distance between the two landmarks, the maps were identical (that is, the physical distance on the map between the bay and the mast was identical). When they were later invited to mentally travel from the telephone mast to the bay, participants in the 80 mile condition took longer than participants in the 20 mile condition. Is this evidence that maps are visually represented or not?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘is this evidence that maps are visually represented?’
Diagnosisevaluate a variant of image scanning (Kosslyn et al., 1978)
Treatmentcompare with the original scanning logic; ask what differs between the two maps (only the number) and what that implies
  • Maps visually identical
  • Only the number differs → time differs
  • Not a visual photocopy
  • Knowledge/propositions shape the scan
  • Analog reply: image built from knowledge
🪝 Memory hook: Same picture, different number, different travel time: knowledge drives the trip.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Mental travel time followed what people knew about the distance, not what they saw.
Tap to open ▸

In Kosslyn’s scanning studies, longer physical distances on the studied map produced longer scan times, taken as evidence for a picture-like (analog) image.

Here the maps were visually identical; only the number (20 vs 80 miles) differed. If people simply scanned a visual copy of the map, scanning times should be equal. They were not.

So this is not evidence for a purely visual representation: the representation (or the scanning process) was influenced by conceptual knowledge of the distance. That fits the propositional critique (Pylyshyn’s ‘tacit knowledge’: people simulate what they know travel should take) and the experimenter/task-demand worries.

An analog theorist can reply that images are constructed from all available knowledge, so the image may encode the represented distance spatially (an analog, not a photographic, code). Either way, the image is not a photocopy of the visual input; meaning shapes it.

Balanced conclusion: the result shows that knowledge, not just visual appearance, determines mental-travel time; it weakens a purely visual interpretation of scanning studies.

  • Answering ‘yes, visual, because time increased’ without noticing the maps were identical.
  • Not linking to Kosslyn et al. (1978).
  • No balanced conclusion.
🐕 Resource D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
🧠 In-depth question · D1

Explain what went wrong or was limited with DVN, and what spatial tapping fixed.

❓ Canvas question D1, word for word
D1In Experiment 1 of the article, dynamical visual noise was used as a distraction task. In Experiment 2 this was changed to the spatial tapping task. What was the reason for this change?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘what was the reason for this change?’
Diagnosismethods question: design choice between experiments
Treatmentdescribe the problem with Exp 1, then show how tapping solves it
  • DVN forced auditory sentences
  • Auditory control: no effect
  • Tapping allows visual sentences
  • Active task = stronger test
  • Bigger sample
🪝 Memory hook: Free the eyes for reading, keep the hands busy for the sketchpad.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The switch made the control condition work and made the distraction harder to ignore.
Tap to open ▸

Problem 1: modality. DVN is a visual display, so in Exp 1 the sentences had to be presented auditorily to the distraction group. The matched auditory control then showed no bizarreness effect, while virtually all earlier research used visual presentation (the visual control did show the effect). You can’t test whether distraction reduces an effect that is absent in the control.

Solution: spatial tapping uses the hands, so sentences can be read on screen in both groups, guaranteeing a robust effect in the control condition.

Problem 2: passivity. DVN only requires looking at flickering squares, with no response. Spatial tapping is an active visuospatial task with repeated responses that may reduce visual working memory more than DVN (Andrade et al., 2002), so it is a more rigorous test of the imagery hypothesis.

They also increased the sample (N = 60) for more power.

  • Saying DVN ‘didn’t work’ without explaining the auditory-control problem.
  • Missing the active vs passive argument.
🐕 Resource D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
🧠 In-depth question · D2

Say which kinds of representation (imaginal, verbal, propositional) can and can’t explain the bizarreness effect after these results.

❓ Canvas question D2, word for word
D2The results of the experiments indicate a very limited role of visual imagery in the bizarreness effect. What does this tell you about the involvement of the different types of mental representation discussed in the first resources of this problem?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘what does this tell you about the different types of representation?’
Diagnosislink a study to theories (dual code, propositional, analog)
Treatmentrule out the imaginal code, then show which codes remain and what that means for the theories
  • Imaginal code: little role
  • Verbal/propositional codes remain
  • Meaning-based elaboration
  • Not anti-imagery (concreteness effect)
  • Selective interference identifies codes
🪝 Memory hook: Block the pictures, keep the meaning: the effect survives, so it lives in the meaning.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The bizarreness effect is carried by meaning-based (verbal/propositional) representations, not images.
Tap to open ▸

The distractors selectively loaded visual/visuospatial working memory and imagery, yet the bizarreness effect was unchanged. So the imaginal (analog) code contributes little to this effect.

What remains are non-imaginal representations: the verbal code of dual-code theory, or abstract propositional/semantic representations of meaning. The authors suggest greater verbal or semantic processing of bizarre sentences (to understand odd relations among the nouns).

This fits the propositional side of the imagery debate for this effect: the sentence’s meaning, e.g. FLOAT(banker, newspaper, puddle), not a picture, is what makes it memorable. In dual-code terms, the benefit sits in the verbal system, not the imaginal one.

It does not show that images don’t exist: DVN does eliminate the concreteness effect (an imagery effect). Different memory effects rely on different representations; selective interference (Brooks, 1968; Segal & Fusella) is the tool to find out which.

  • Concluding imagery doesn’t exist at all.
  • Not naming the theories from Resources A–C.
  • Ignoring the concreteness-effect contrast.
🐕 Resource D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
🧠 In-depth question · D3

Name the working-memory component the distractors were chosen to load.

❓ Canvas question D3, word for word
D3The authors use a visual and a spatial distractor task in Experiment 1 and Experiment 2, respectively. Based on this choice of distractor tasks, which component of Baddeley’s working memory model do you think they PRESUME is involved in the bizarreness effect?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘which component … do they PRESUME?’
Diagnosislink methods to Baddeley & Hitch’s working-memory model
Treatmentidentify what DVN and tapping load, and what they leave free
  • Model: CE, loop, sketchpad
  • DVN → visual cache
  • Tapping → spatial (inner scribe)
  • Loop deliberately spared
  • Presumed: visuo-spatial sketchpad
🪝 Memory hook: Jam the sketchpad, leave the loop: test the picture route only.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The design assumes the bizarreness effect, if imagery-based, runs through the visuo-spatial sketchpad.
Tap to open ▸

Baddeley & Hitch’s model has a central executive, a phonological loop and a visuo-spatial sketchpad (later also an episodic buffer).

DVN loads the visual part of the sketchpad (visual cache); spatial tapping loads its spatial part (inner scribe); the visual span task (Exp 3–4) loads visual storage. None of them should affect the phonological loop or verbal processing, which is why sentences can still be read and understood.

So they presume visual imagery for bizarre sentences is generated and held in the visuo-spatial sketchpad: if the bizarreness effect were imagery-based, loading the sketchpad should reduce it.

Footnote 1 says the tasks come from this model; the authors add that newer work questions a separate visual store (Morey, 2018), but their test only needs tasks that selectively impair visuospatial processing.

  • Answering ‘phonological loop’.
  • Not explaining what each task loads.
  • Forgetting the central executive is (meant to be) minimally loaded.
🐕 Resource D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
🧠 In-depth question · D4

Use what you know about semantic memory to explain why bizarre scenes are harder to picture vividly.

❓ Canvas question D4, word for word
D4Why are the vividness ratings of the bizarre sentences lower compared to those of the common sentences? [Hint: Your knowledge of the previous problem on semantic memory might come in handy here.]
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘why lower vividness? hint: semantic memory’
Diagnosisapply semantic-memory concepts (networks, schemas, typicality) to a result
Treatmentexplain how common scenes are supported by stored knowledge and bizarre ones aren’t
  • Bizarre: lower and slower vividness
  • Common scenes match schemas & networks
  • Strong associations → fluent rich image
  • Bizarre: no stored links, built from scratch
  • Weaker image yet better memory
🪝 Memory hook: Your memory has a photo album of dogs chasing bikes, not of dogs riding them.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Familiar scenes are easy to picture because semantic memory already holds them; bizarre ones must be built.
Tap to open ▸

Result: in all experiments bizarre sentences got lower vividness ratings (e.g. 2.99 vs 3.58) and slower rating RTs than common sentences.

Semantic memory explanation: common scenes (‘the dog chased the bicycle’) match existing schemas/scripts, prototypes and strongly associated concepts in the semantic network (spreading activation from dog → chase). Retrieving and assembling such an image is fluent and draws on many stored details, so it feels vivid.

Bizarre scenes (‘the dog rode the bicycle’) combine concepts that have no stored links and violate world knowledge. There is no ready-made representation to retrieve, so the image must be constructed from parts, with more transformations, takes longer and is less complete; it feels less vivid.

Implication: bizarre items are the weaker imagery condition, yet they are remembered better, which argues against the account that bizarre sentences are better remembered because they produce stronger/more elaborated images (the authors’ point).

  • Ignoring the semantic-memory hint.
  • Saying bizarre images are ‘more distinctive, so more vivid’ (the data show the opposite).
  • Not linking to the imagery account.
🐕 Resource D · Besken & Mulligan (2021)
🧠 In-depth question · D5

Look at the vividness numbers with and without distraction, judge whether imagery was really disrupted, and decide whether you accept the conclusion.

❓ Canvas question D5, word for word
D5Have you noticed that the experiments contain a contradictory element? While the distractor tasks are meant to disrupt and perhaps prevent the formation of visual imagery, participants are still expected to rate the vividness of their mental images. Inspect the absolute vividness ratings in Table 1 and decide whether the distractor tasks had the intended effects. Do you agree with the authors’ conclusion about the limited role of visual imagery in the bizarreness effect?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘inspect Table 1 … intended effects? do you agree?’
Diagnosisevaluate a manipulation check and a conclusion
Treatmentread the numbers, judge the manipulation, weigh the authors’ counter-arguments, give a reasoned verdict
  • Ratings not lower under distraction
  • Manipulation check questionable
  • Authors: slower RTs, validated tasks
  • Between-subjects ratings insensitive
  • Partly agree: limited role, not zero
🪝 Memory hook: If the lights were supposedly off, why did people still see clearly?
★ KEY INSIGHT · Unchanged vividness ratings weaken, but don’t overturn, the conclusion that imagery plays a limited role.
Tap to open ▸

Table 1: vividness ratings were not lower under distraction: Exp 1 DVN 3.01/3.84 vs controls 2.99/3.58 and 2.91/4.01; Exp 2 tapping 3.36/4.17 vs control 2.82/4.06 (higher!); Exp 3 span 3.10/3.96 vs 2.92/4.03. If the distractors had prevented imagery, ratings should have dropped.

So, judged by the ratings, the manipulation did not clearly work: participants still reported vivid images. That is a problem: the conclusion ‘imagery plays little role’ assumes imagery was disrupted. If it wasn’t, an unchanged bizarreness effect says little.

The authors’ counter-arguments: (1) the tasks are validated selective disruptors in earlier research (e.g. DVN eliminates the concreteness effect); (2) vividness RTs were slower under distraction in Exp 1–3 (e.g. 1,106 vs 839 ms), suggesting harder imaging; (3) in a between-subjects design people can’t compare their image with an undistracted one, so ratings may not shift; (4) in Exp 3–4 the distractor did lower overall recall, yet not the bizarreness effect.

Verdict (one defensible answer): partly agree. The convergent nulls across four tasks plus Bayes factors (BF01 ≈ 11–14) make a large imagery contribution unlikely, but the vividness data mean imagery may have been only partly disrupted; a within-subject manipulation check, an objective imagery measure, or a stronger (manipulation-based) visual task would make the conclusion firmer.

  • Not quoting numbers from Table 1.
  • Only agreeing or disagreeing without weighing the authors’ arguments.
  • Confusing vividness ratings with recall.

Block A–C · How Are Mental Images Represented?

❓ In what format are mental images stored: as picture-like analog representations, or as abstract propositions?

👁️A.1

What mental imagery is, and why it is hard to study

❓ This lecture answers: What counts as mental imagery, why does it matter, and why can't we just ask people about their images?
A.1.1
Pictures in the mind

🖼️ Mental imagery: representing what is not currently sensed (Moulton & Kosslyn, 2009), in any sense, but research focuses on visual imagery (Kosslyn et al., 1990). Used for problem solving, therapy and memory; skill varies (Reisberg et al., 1986), even on fMRI (Cui et al., 2007).

A.1.2
A banned topic, and a hard one

🚫 Wundt valued imagery (Palmer, 1999); Watson denied it, so only 34 articles in 1950–59. Hard to study: images can't be observed, fade fast, and self-reports mislead (Anderson, 1998; Pylyshyn, 2006). Storing every image as a copy would overflow the brain.

📺
THINK OF IT LIKE…A TV that can play from the antenna (perception) or from a recording (imagery). Same screen, different source. The question for the rest of this block: is the "recording" a video file (picture-like) or a script describing the scene (proposition)?
TRY IT · 30 SECONDS

🍒 Use your mind's eye

Answer each question, then notice HOW you answered.

Click an answer.
A.1.1 · TAP TO OPEN

🧰 Imagery at work: the uses in your reading

Tap each use to see the study behind it.

👆 Tap a button to open it.
Which is darker red, a cherry or an apple? How many windows does your home have? How do the pieces of a puzzle fit? Kosslyn: we answer by visualising the objects (Kosslyn & Rabin, 1999; Kosslyn, Thompson & Ganis, 2006).
Guided imagery helps control pain, strengthen immune responses and treat phobias and anxiety. In occupational therapy, brain-damaged patients imagine the steps of a task in order, which helps them wash dishes or take medication (Liu & Chan, 2009).
People with Down syndrome remembered a story better when they formed images while hearing it (de la Iglesia, Buceta & Campos, 2005; Kihara & Yoshikawa, 2001).
Practising with mental images of three lines made people more sensitive to their asymmetry (Tartaglia et al., 2009). Architects not allowed to sketch simply used mental images, with no effect on their designs (Bilda, 2006).
Imagery skill differs between people (Reisberg et al., 1986; Schienle et al., 2008), and the differences are even visible with fMRI (Cui et al., 2007).
Yes. Schools rarely teach spatial imagery and many students think they cannot improve, but training improves spatial performance at any age (Ganis et al., 2009; Reed, 2010; Newcombe, 2010).
✗ THE MISTAKE"The analog view says there's a photo in your head."
✓ CORRECTSupporters of analog coding explicitly do not claim a literal picture (Ganis et al., 2009; Kosslyn et al., 2006). The claim: the representation preserves the spatial relations of the object, like a picture does.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDMental imagery is seeing, hearing or smelling something that isn't there, like picturing your front door. It's useful for problem-solving, therapy and memory. But it's really hard to study, because nobody can look inside your head, and people are bad at describing their own thinking.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKImage = seeing without seeing.
✎ EXAM TIPKnow why introspection is not enough (no conscious access; inaccurate self-reports) and that researchers therefore measure behaviour, such as reaction times, borrowed from perception research.
▶ Find a video: mental imagery explained
✅ Quick check: Why did the behaviourists reject imagery research?

Because images can't be linked to observable behaviour; Watson even argued imagery didn't exist. As a result, North American psychologists rarely studied imagery from 1920 to 1960.

🧩A.2

Two theories: dual codes or propositions?

❓ This lecture answers: Do we store images AND words (Paivio), or only abstract meanings (Pylyshyn)?
A.2.1
Dual-code theory: images and symbols

🧩 Paivio: two codes. Analog codes resemble things (an analog clock); a symbolic code is chosen arbitrarily (the numeral "9"). Paivio (1969): pictures recalled best in any order, words in sequence. Brooks (1968): a same-code response slows you down.

A.2.2
Propositional theory: one abstract code

💭 Pylyshyn; Anderson & Bower (1973): only propositions ("mentalese") are stored, shown in predicate calculus: relation(subject, object). A proposition is neither words nor images (Clark & Chase, 1972); experienced images are epiphenomena.

A.2.3
The imagery debate

⚖️ The imagery debate (Kosslyn et al., 2006): do images resemble perception (analog) or language (a propositional code; Pylyshyn, 2003, 2006)? Most favour analog: imagery activates the primary visual cortex, and >90% of brain areas are shared with seeing.

TRY IT · CONCRETE VS ABSTRACT

📝 The dual-coding memory test

Study Sternberg's 8 words for 15 seconds. Then tick the ones you remember (4 extra words are lures illustrative). Dual-code theory predicts you'll get more concrete words (they can be stored as a picture AND a word).

Words appear here
