🧱 Build a proposition

Choose an agent, a relation and an object. See the same fact in all three formats.

A.2.3 · THE IMAGERY DEBATE

⚖️ Analog or propositional? Weigh the evidence

The imagery debate (Kosslyn et al., 2006). Tap each finding to see which side it supports.

Do images resemble PERCEPTION or LANGUAGE?
🖼️ ANALOG (most theorists)
close relative of perception (Tversky, 2005)
a triangle image keeps its spatial relations
Kosslyn · Howes (2007) · Reisberg et al. (2003)
not a literal picture in the head
📝 PROPOSITIONAL CODE
abstract, language-like description
neither visual nor spatial
Pylyshyn (2003, 2006) · Ganis et al. (2009) · Reed (2010)
can be used to generate an image
👆 Tap a button to open it.
Tasks that need detailed visual imagery activate the primary visual cortex, the same area used to see real objects (Ganis et al., 2009). → supports analog.
People with prosopagnosia, who cannot recognise faces visually, have comparable problems creating images of faces (Farah, 2004; Ganis et al., 2009). → supports analog.
In Kosslyn's lab, more than 90% of the brain areas used to classify parts of visible (degraded) objects were also used for imagined objects. → supports analog.
Early visual cortex was active during imagery only when (1) the task needed high-resolution detail (an animal's ears: yes), (2) it was visual rather than spatial (which arm holds the Statue of Liberty's torch: no), and (3) a more powerful scanner was used.
Imagining twisting an object by hand activates motor areas; imagining an external force rotating it does not. So imagery is "not one thing" but a collection of abilities (Kosslyn).
Hard to resolve. Most imagery researchers favour the analog view, perhaps partly because they personally experience vivid images (Reisberg et al., 2003). Both views are probably partly correct, depending on the task.
🗂️
THINK OF IT LIKE…A photo 📷, its caption 🏷️, and the index card in the archive that both are made from 🗂️. Paivio: we keep photos and captions. Pylyshyn: there are only index cards, and the photo is printed fresh each time you look.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Propositional theory denies that people experience images."
✓ CORRECTIt accepts that we experience images, but says they are epiphenomena re-created from an abstract code; the stored format is propositional, not pictorial.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDThere are two big ideas about what's in your head. Either you store pictures and words separately, like a photo album plus a diary, or you store only abstract meanings and your brain re-creates the picture or the sentence when you need it.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKTwo codes (Paivio) vs one meaning code (Pylyshyn).
✎ EXAM TIPUse Sternberg's Table 7.1 (cat under the table) to show what a proposition is, and Brooks (1968) as the classic dual-code experiment.
▶ Find a video: dual-coding theory📚 Read: dual-coding theory overview
✅ Quick check: Why are concrete words recalled better than abstract ones?

Concrete words (book, hat) are easy to visualise, so they can be stored in BOTH codes; abstract words (peace, harmony) mostly in the verbal code only. Two routes to recall beat one. Sternberg calls this a demonstration of the dual-coding hypothesis, or its modern version, the functional-equivalence hypothesis (A.3).

🔄A.3

Testing the debate: functional equivalence and mental rotation

❓ This lecture answers: How can you test the format of something invisible? And what does rotating a mental image reveal?
A.3.1
The logic of functional equivalence

⚖️ Functional-equivalence hypothesis (Hubbard, 2010): if images resemble objects, we should judge them in the same way: rotate, scan, compare shapes, feel interference. Behaves like perception → analog view; doesn't → propositional view.

A.3.2
Shepard and Metzler’s mental rotation study

🧊 8 participants judged 1,600 pairs of 3-D block figures: same or different? DV = reaction time. Time rose linearly with angle; depth ≈ flat. A description predicts equal times for 20° and 160° (Howes, 2007).

A.3.3
Replications, individual differences and the brain

🧠 Replicated with letters and hands: upright hands beat upside-down ones (Takeda et al., 2010). Rotating by hand first → primary motor cortex (Kosslyn, Thompson et al., 2001). Training shrinks gender differences.

INTERACTIVE EXPERIMENT · ~1 MINUTE

🔄 Run your own Shepard & Metzler

Is the right letter the same as the left one (just rotated) or a mirror image? Answer as fast as you can. After 16 trials your own reaction times are plotted against angle.

R
R
Trial 0 / 16
A.3.3 · TAP TO OPEN

🧠 Who rotates how? Replications, people and brains

Rotation is "not one thing". Tap each card.

Kosslyn, Thompson et al. (2001): how you met the figure matters
✋ rotate it by hand
later mental rotation (PET):
primary motor cortex ON
⚙️ watch an electric motor
later mental rotation (PET):
motor cortex not active
👆 Tap a button to open it.
Left or right hand? People recognise upright hands faster and more accurately than upside-down hands, because 0° is quicker than 180° (Takeda et al., 2010). Right-handers were faster for right hands; left-handers equally fast for both.
Elderly people rotate more slowly than young people, although age is not consistently related to other imagery skills such as sense of direction or scanning (e.g., Dror & Kosslyn, 1994).
Deaf people fluent in American Sign Language are especially good at rotating a scene by 180° (Emmorey et al., 1998), probably because they constantly rotate a narrator's signs to match their own perspective.
Women show extra inferior frontal activation and use both hemispheres; men mainly the right (Hugdahl et al., 2006). Women's proportionally more parietal grey matter goes with more effort (Koscik et al., 2009). Training reduces or eliminates the difference (Bosco, Longoni & Vecchi, 2004).
"Rotate the figure" activates right frontal and parietal lobes (Wraga et al., 2005; Zacks et al., 2001). "Imagine rotating yourself around it" adds left temporal and motor-cortex activity (Kosslyn et al., 2001; Wraga et al., 2005). Wording changes how the brain does the task.
Watching virtual-reality figures rotate can stimulate the motor cortex of stroke patients and shorten the time before they make actual movements (Ganis et al., 2009).
🧳
THINK OF IT LIKE…Checking whether your suitcase fits in the boot: you "turn" it in your head, and a half turn takes longer than a quarter turn. A written list ("blue case, 70 cm") would take the same time however it was turned.
Mental rotation time grows in a straight line with the angle, just as with real objects: the strongest single piece of evidence that images preserve spatial properties, as the analog view claims.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Rotation studies measure how accurately people judge the figures."
✓ CORRECTThe key dependent variable is reaction time as a function of the angle.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDIf you're asked whether two weird block shapes are the same, you turn one in your head, and the more you have to turn it, the longer it takes, exactly like turning a real object. That's hard to explain if your brain just stores a description.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKMore degrees, more seconds.
✎ EXAM TIPState the prediction of each theory explicitly: analog predicts time rising with angle; propositional predicts no relation. Then give the result: linear increase (Shepard & Metzler, 1971).
▶ Find a video: mental rotation experiment🧪 Another online rotation demo
✅ Quick check: A pilot compares a map rotated 150° vs 30°. Which is faster?

30°. Mental rotation time increases with the angle, as with physically turning the map.

🔍A.4

Size, distance and shape in the mind's eye

❓ This lecture answers: Do imagined size, distance and shape behave like the real thing, and could researchers' expectations explain the results?
A.4.1
Image scaling: zooming in on mental images

🐘 Kosslyn (1975) used relative size: a rabbit beside an elephant is small on the "mental screen", so its features take longer. Kosslyn (1976): imagery condition → larger features faster; non-imagery condition → distinctive features faster.

A.4.2
Image scanning: distance in the mind’s eye

🏝️ Island map: scan time rose almost perfectly linearly with distance (Kosslyn, Ball & Reiser, 1978), as in perception (Denis & Kosslyn, 1999). Also with dots (Borst & Kosslyn, 2008) and a 3-D box of toys (Pinker, 1980). Propositions (Pylyshyn, 1973) predict no distance effect.

A.4.3
The experimenter-expectancy objection

🕵️ Did researchers' expectations leak to participants (Intons-Peterson, 1983)? Jolicoeur & Kosslyn (1985b) gave naive assistants a convincing but wrong U-shaped prediction: they still got a straight line.

A.4.4
Shape: mental clocks and mental maps

🕰️ Paivio (1978): comparing imagined clock angles is slow when they are similar; high-imagery people are faster than low-imagery people. U.S. state shapes are judged alike from names and from sketches (Shepard & Chipman, 1970).

INTERACTIVE · IMAGE SCANNING

🏝️ Scan your mental island

1) Study the island for a few seconds. 2) Press Hide map. 3) For each pair, picture a dot travelling from the first landmark to the second and press Arrived! when it gets there. Your times are plotted against the real distance.

Study the map first.
Matlin's three conclusions so far: (1) a large rotation of an image takes longer, as with physical objects; (2) distance judgements are similar for images and physical stimuli; (3) shape judgements are similar, for simple shapes (clock angles) and complex ones (states).
📱
THINK OF IT LIKE…A photo on your phone: you pinch to zoom in for detail, and scrolling further takes longer. Your mental image seems to follow the same rules.
✗ THE MISTAKE"The linear scanning result alone proves images are spatial."
✓ CORRECTThe result could in principle come from expectations or knowledge rather than the image itself. Jolicoeur & Kosslyn (1985b) ruled out experimenter expectancy, which is why their control study matters.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDMental images act like real pictures: tiny things in your imagination are harder to inspect, travelling farther across an imagined map takes longer, and comparing similar imagined clock angles is slow, just like with real clocks. And no, it's not because the researchers hinted at the answer.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKBigger = clearer; farther = slower; similar = slower.
✎ EXAM TIPFor scanning, always add the control: Jolicoeur and Kosslyn (1985b) gave naive assistants a false U-shaped prediction and still got a linear result.
▶ Find a video: Kosslyn's island map
✅ Quick check: Mouse next to a horse vs next to a matchbox. When do you "see" its whiskers faster?

Next to the matchbox: there the mouse is relatively large in the image, so its details are easier to inspect (Kosslyn, 1975).

✡️A.5

Interference, ambiguous figures and representational neglect

❓ This lecture answers: Does imagery compete with seeing, and where do images fail to behave like pictures?
A.5.1
Imagery interferes with seeing

🌳 Segal & Fusella (1970): imagining a tree made a faint arrow harder to detect; imagining an oboe did not (same sense only). Imagined lines bias judgements of a real line, like real lines do (Mast et al., 1999).

A.5.2
Ambiguous figures: where images do not behave like pictures

✡️ Reed (1974): the parallelogram hidden in an imagined Star of David was found only 14% of the time (55% overall; chance 50%) → pictures are sometimes stored as descriptions. Can people reinterpret an imagined duck/rabbit? Your Matlin excerpt ends here.

A.5.3
Representational neglect

🧭 Spatial neglect: ignoring half the visual field. Representational neglect: ignoring half of an imagined scene (Peru & Zapparoli, 1999). Patients describe a seen image fully but omit its left side from memory (Denis et al., 2002; Logie et al., 2005).

INTERACTIVE · REED (1974)

✡️ Find the hidden shape in your mind

You'll see a figure for 3 seconds. Then it disappears and a part appears. Was that part in the figure? Answer from your mental image only.

Most evidence (rotation, scanning, size, shape, interference, neglect) says images behave like perception, but ambiguous figures show that images are also partly stored as descriptions, so both codes are probably used, depending on the task.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Reed proved mental images don't exist."
✓ CORRECTReed concluded that people sometimes store pictures as propositional descriptions. Matlin's overall verdict: both analog and propositional codes are probably used, depending on the task.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDImagining something can block you from seeing something real, because both use the same equipment. But images aren't perfect pictures: picture a Star of David and try to find a parallelogram in it. Most people can't, which suggests they stored 'two triangles' as a description.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKImages compete with seeing, but can't always be re-read.
✎ EXAM TIPGive one piece of evidence for each side: analog (Shepard & Metzler; Kosslyn; Segal & Fusella) and propositional (Reed, 1974), and conclude that both codes are used depending on the task.
▶ Find a video: duck–rabbit and mental images▶ Find a video: representational neglect
✅ Quick check: Why do Segal & Fusella need the oboe condition?

It shows the interference is specific to the same sense. Without it, the tree result might just mean "any extra task makes detection worse".

Besken & Mulligan (2021), JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition

Block D · Is the Bizarreness Effect Visual?

❓ Is the memory advantage for bizarre sentences caused by visual imagery, or by something else?

🐕D.1

The bizarreness effect and the imagery question

❓ This lecture answers: What is the bizarreness effect, why was it credited to imagery, and how can we test that?
D.1.1
A strange sentence is easier to remember

🐕🚲 Mixed list: "The dog rode the bicycle" beats "The dog chased…" (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986): the bizarreness effect, or bizarre imagery effect. Visual-imagery hypothesis: more elaboration (Wollen & Margres, 1987) or more distinctiveness (Black et al., 2012).

D.1.2
Reasons for doubt, and why earlier studies could not decide

🤔 The effect appears without imagery instructions (Hirshman et al., 1989; Weir & Richman, 1996); less vivid imagers show a larger effect (Anderson & Buyer, 1994) → verbal elaboration? But sentences allow both codes and instructions only reduce imagery.

D.1.3
The better test: block imagery and see what happens

🔧 Disrupting visual imagery during encoding should shrink a visual effect. Tool: a task that loads the visuo-spatial sketchpad (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974; Logie et al., 1990), not the phonological loop or the central executive.

D.1.1–D.1.2 · TAP TO OPEN

🧱 Why imagery was assumed, and why earlier studies could not decide

An old idea, now tested in the lab. Tap each reason.

📜 90 BCE
Ad Herennium: use ridiculous, fantastic images to keep memories
📚 Self-help books
Buzan (1991); Lorayne & Lucas (1974); Lorayne (2010)
🧑‍⚕️ Memory training
Dalgleish et al. (2013); Matzen et al. (2016)
🔬 Lab effect
McDaniel & Einstein (1986); only with imagery instructions? (Burns, 1996)
👆 Tap a button to open it.
Sentences can be encoded as images and as words. Even when people formed images from nouns, they usually described them aloud, which again involves words.
Someone reading "the dog rode the bicycle" may picture it anyway. Non-imagery instructions only reduce imagery, and the effect is generally reduced too, which is what the imagery hypothesis predicts.
In Worthen (1997), the sentence condition's bizarreness effect was numerically less than half the size of the imagery conditions' effects, despite a non-significant interaction. And correlations (Anderson & Buyer, 1994) cannot show cause and effect.
They did not use selective tasks: Worthen et al. (2000) used a "press any key" attention task with no no-distraction condition; Gounden & Nicolas (2012) used an auditory odd-number task that loads the central executive, not visual working memory.
INTERACTIVE · YOUR OWN BIZARRENESS EFFECT

🐕🚲 Mini memory experiment

Ten sentences appear for 4 seconds each (a mix of bizarre and common; written for this demo illustrative, in the style of McDaniel & Einstein). Picture each one. Then count backwards for 20 seconds, and recall: tick the sentences you remember.

Sentences appear here
🤨
THINK OF IT LIKE…A friend tells you "my dog rode my bike". You stop and think "wait, how?". That moment of working out the meaning, not a mental picture, may be what makes it stick.
✗ THE MISTAKE"It's called the bizarre imagery effect, so imagery must cause it."
✓ CORRECTThe label reflects the traditional explanation. Whether imagery causes the effect is exactly what Besken & Mulligan test, and their answer is: very little.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDWeird sentences like 'the dog rode the bicycle' are easier to remember than normal ones. Everyone assumed that's because you form a vivid, weird mental picture. But earlier studies couldn't prove it, because sentences also involve words and meaning. So the trick is to block people's visual imagery while they read and see if the advantage disappears.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKBlock the picture, watch the effect.
✎ EXAM TIPName the two imagery versions (elaboration; distinctiveness) and the alternative (verbal/semantic elaboration), and explain why selective interference is a stronger, causal test than instructions or correlations.
▶ Find a video: the bizarreness effect▶ Find a video: working memory model📄 The article (DOI)
✅ Quick check: Why would counting backwards aloud be a poor distractor here?

It loads verbal processing (phonological loop), not visual imagery. A selective test needs a task that occupies the visuo-spatial sketchpad while leaving verbal processing free.

🧪D.2

Four experiments, one answer

❓ This lecture answers: Did blocking visual imagery shrink the bizarreness effect?
REAL DATA · BESKEN & MULLIGAN TABLES 2–5

📊 Did distraction shrink the bizarre advantage?

Choose an experiment. Bars = proportion of sentences accessed. The number on top is the bizarreness effect (bizarre − common).

In Exps 3 and 4 the span task gave a main effect of group (lower recall overall). Span accuracy was .75 (chance .50), equal for bizarre and common trials. In Exp 4, noun recall showed only a non-significant trend for bizarreness (p = .075), not unusual with non-vividness ratings (Kroll & Tu, 1988; Worthen, 1997).

D.2.1
The shared design

🧪 Study phase: a mixed list of 8 bizarre + 8 common sentences (e.g. banker, newspaper, puddle). Sentence type within, distraction between participants. Surprise recall scored as sentence access and noun recall; the key test is the interaction.

D.2.2
Experiment 1: dynamic visual noise

📺 DVN (TV static) while hearing sentences (n = 36). The visual control showed a clear effect (d = 1.18); with DVN it was even larger (d = 1.70), but the auditory control showed none (only earlier auditory study: Anderson & Buyer, 1994).

D.2.3
Experiment 2: spatial tapping

✋ 60 people tapped a diamond pattern without looking, which disrupts visuospatial but not verbal processing (Salway & Logie, 1995; Baddeley & Andrade, 2000). Effect .17 with tapping vs .16 without: no interaction (p = .85).

D.2.4
Experiments 3 and 4: the visual span task

🏁 Visual span task: keep in mind a 5 × 6 checkerboard (Logie et al., 1990). Experiment 3 (vividness ratings) and Experiment 4 (plausibility ratings): recall fell overall, but for bizarre and common sentences equally (p = .68; p = .42).

D.2.5
Combined, meta-analytic and Bayesian analyses

⚖️ Null interactions need backing. Pooled power .98: interaction p = .27, any trend the wrong way. BF01 = 11.49 and 13.86 (above 3 favours "no change"). A single-paper meta-analysis agrees.

D.2.6
What it means, and what it does not mean

🧠 The effect was never reduced, so visual imagery plays little role. The same DVN shrinks the concreteness effect (Parker & Dagnall, 2009): different bases. Best fit: verbal or semantic elaboration; the process of trying to image, not the image.

D.2.6 · TAP TO OPEN

🧩 What it means, and what it does not mean

Four questions the authors answer.

👆 Tap a button to open it.
Why didn't vividness ratings drop under distraction? (1) The tasks are well established as impairing visuospatial processing. (2) Rating times were slower under distraction (Exps 1–3), normally a sign of harder imaging. (3) Distraction was between participants, so nobody could compare (Susser et al., 2013). Bizarre sentences were rated less vivid, which makes the elaboration version unlikely; the distinctiveness version predicts a shrinking effect, which never happened.
Unlikely: the same DVN reduces the concreteness effect in long-term memory (Parker & Dagnall, 2009; Chubala et al., 2018). So the concreteness effect (imagery-based) and the bizarreness effect must have different bases.
Verbal or semantic elaboration: the distractors leave meaning processing intact, and the effect survived. Picturing a bizarre scene forces you to understand each word and how they relate; a plausibility judgement only needs to notice that it's odd (and was faster). So the process of trying to form the image matters, not the image itself. For bizarre pictures this remains speculation.
An effect long credited to imagery may rest on verbal and semantic representations, consistent with a propositional basis. But the authors do not draw broad conclusions against imagery-based representations: the result concerns one effect.
FEEL IT · DYNAMIC VISUAL NOISE

📺 Try imaging through the static

Read the sentence, close your eyes partly, and try to picture it while the static flickers (each square changes with probability .5 every 0.25 s, as in Experiment 1). Notice: you can still understand what it means.

"The banker floated across the puddle on a newspaper."
Four experiments, three distractors and a Bayes factor above 11 agree: disrupting visual imagery never shrinks the bizarreness effect, so the "bizarre imagery effect" is mainly a matter of meaning, not pictures.
🎬
THINK OF IT LIKE…Turning off the projector didn't stop the film, so the film wasn't coming from the projector. Blocking pictures didn't shrink the bizarre bonus, so the bonus isn't coming from pictures.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Besken & Mulligan disproved mental imagery, or dual-code theory."
✓ CORRECTThey showed that one effect, the bizarreness effect for sentences, does not depend on visual imagery. The same distractors do reduce the concreteness effect, so imagery exists as a separate code; it just does not drive this effect.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDResearchers made people watch TV-static, tap a hidden pattern, or hold a checkerboard in mind while reading weird and normal sentences. That should block mental pictures. But the weird sentences were still remembered better, by the same amount. So the bizarre-memory trick is about thinking through the meaning, not about seeing a picture.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKBlock the picture, the bonus stays: it's meaning, not images.
✎ EXAM TIPAlways describe the result as an interaction: the main effect of bizarreness stayed, distraction sometimes lowered recall overall, but the bizarre-minus-common difference did not shrink (pooled p = .27; BF01 ≈ 11–14).
▶ Find a video: dynamic visual noise▶ Find a video: Bayes factors, simply
✅ Quick check: Why did Exp 4 use plausibility instead of vividness ratings?

To remove the explicit instruction to form images, in case that instruction helped people image despite the distractor. The effect still wasn't reduced.

✅ Quick check: Distraction lowered recall in Exps 3–4. So did it reduce the bizarreness effect?

No. Distraction lowered recall overall (a main effect), but the bizarre − common difference did not change (no interaction). Only a smaller difference would point to imagery.

✅ Quick check: Why did the authors add Bayesian and meta-analytic analyses?

Because a non-significant interaction on its own is weak evidence: it might reflect too little power. Pooled power (.98), Bayes factors (BF01 = 11.49 and 13.86) and a single-paper meta-analysis show positive evidence that the effect is not smaller under distraction.

⚖️ Synthesis: weighing the evidence

Test what a representation does: if imagined size, distance and angle cost time like the real thing, the image is analog; if knocking out imagery leaves an effect untouched, that effect runs on meaning.

📄 Theme 5 on one page

👁️A1

What imagery is

Seeing without the stimulus; useful, varies between people; hard to study → measure behaviour, not reports.
🧩A2

Two theories

Dual code: images + words (Paivio, Brooks). Propositional: only meanings; images are side effects (Pylyshyn).
🔄A3

Mental rotation

Bigger turn → longer time, in a straight line (Shepard & Metzler, 1971). Strongest analog evidence.
🔍A4

Size, distance, shape

Small = slow detail; far = slow scan (not expectancy); similar angles = slow. Images keep spatial properties.
✡️A5

Interference, Reed, neglect

Same-sense imagery blocks seeing; hidden parallelogram found 14% → some images are descriptions; neglect of imagined halves.
🐕D1

The bizarreness question

Bizarre sentences remembered better; imagery assumed but doubted. Test: block imagery during encoding.
🧪D2

Four experiments

Static, tapping, checkerboard: the bizarre advantage never shrank (pooled p = .27; BF01 ≈ 11–14). Meaning, not pictures.
💬 The whole theme to a friend: "Psychologists argue whether pictures in your head are real pictures or descriptions dressed up as pictures. Mostly they act like pictures: turning them takes longer for bigger turns and crossing a mental map takes longer for longer distances. But you can't always find hidden shapes in them, so some are descriptions. And the famous trick that weird images help memory? Block the pictures and it still works, so it's really about meaning."

Sources: Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio, Cognitive Psychology, Ch. 7 · Matlin, Cognition, Ch. 7 · Besken & Mulligan (2021), JEP:LMC. Video buttons open a YouTube search, so you can choose a current video.
